Material and methods
Study location, animals and breeding practices
The data were collected over 26 years (1993-2016) by the Office de I’Elevage et des Paturages from its Jebibina-Saouef breed- ing farm located in Central Tunisia. The farm belongs to the Saouef subdistrict where the mean annual temperature is 18.1 °C and annual rainfall is 366 mm (Climate data.org, 2023). Temperature and precipitation were recorded here for 40 years, including the 26 years of the study period (Fig. 1). Long-term dynamics of Nor- malised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) were gathered from satellite missions Advanced Very High-Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR) (Fig. 1) and annual NDVI values were considered.
The animals were of the fat-tailed Barbarine breed (Atti and Bocquier, 1999; Ben Salem et al., 2011). The farm has nine Bar- barine ﬂocks, each comprising 250–300 ewes. The ﬂocks were housed outdoors year-round and grazed on natural and improved rangeland. In addition to grazing, the animals received supple- ments of hay (0.5–1 kg/head/day) and concentrates (200–300 g/h ead/day) during mating, late gestation, and beginning of lactation. Flocks were annually vaccinated against foot and mouth disease, brucellosis, and sheep pox and regularly received preventive antiparasitic treatments. Annually, breeding male lambs were selected at age 6 months on their growth performances using a Best Linear Predictor index. This index was also used for the selec- tion of replacement ewe lambs. Selected ewe lambs were kept as replacement and reared in complete isolation from rams starting from age 6 months postweaning. At age 18 months, immediately before they were ﬁrst mated, 40–50 of the maiden ewes were rein- troduced in each ﬂock. All ﬂocks were mated in spring every year, with rams introduced to all ﬂocks on the same day between 20 April and 10 May. On average, six rams were used for every 100 ewes, and ewes in all ﬂocks were totally isolated from rams for at least 6 weeks before joining. As a general practice, shepherd assistance is required to lift the tail at the time of copulation. This allows a full record of oestrus occurrences (twice a day) for each mating combination. As some rams can lift the fat tail without any help and mate and as in the studied farm, pedigree data are systematically recorded, the rams are usually separated from the females at night to prevent any uncontrolled mating events. All ewes were weighed prior to mating season, constantly exposed
to natural photoperiod, and received no hormonal treatment.

Analysis of non-genetic effects
Multinomial regression analysis was employed using the ‘multinom’ function from the ‘nnet’ package in R software (R Core Team, 2023) to examine the relationship between oestrus response: Cyre (used as reference), Cylate, Cyspon, and Cynull and the non-genetic factors of variation. Model ﬁxed effects were year (levels 1993–2016) and ﬂock (levels 1–9); weight was a covariate to determine any signiﬁcant associations between inde- pendent variables (year, ﬂock, and weight) and categories of oes- trus response.
Binomial regression analysis was conducted using GLM func- tion from the base R package for binary logistic regression to inves- tigate the effects of independent variables on fertility and litter size. Model ﬁxed effects were year (1993–2016), ﬂock (1–9), and oestrus response (Cyspon, Cyre, and Cylate). Cynull level was not valid in litter size and fertility analysis, as there was no litter size record for Cynull and all were not fertile by default. Weight was a covariate to determine whether independent variables had a sig- niﬁcant inﬂuence on fertility and litter size as well as to estimate the odds ratio (OR) for different categories within the oestrus response and ﬁxed effect levels.

Discussion
This study revealed that maiden Barbarine ewes were not totally sexually inactive during spring anoestrus months. Similar patterns were reported by De Lucas and Garcia (1991) for maiden Merino Rambouillet ewes in Mexico. However, comparisons should be considered cautiously because of age differences in what is des- ignated as nulliparous females. Capacity of sheep for out-of-season sexual activity was demonstrated in Barbarine (Tunisia; Maatoug- Ouzini et al., 2013), Mérinos d’Arles (France; Hanocq et al., 1999) and Chios ewes (Greece; Avdi et al., 2003) - these correspond to Mediterranean latitudes where the ‘ram effect’ proved an efficient management practice to trigger out-of-season female reproductive activity (Lassoued, 1998). In our study, spontaneous cyclicity (24%) and response to ‘ram effect’ of non—cyclic maiden ewes (50.45%) were lower than for multiparous Barbarine ewes (28 and 86%, respectively; Maatoug-Ouzini et al., 2013). Introduction
Sheep breeds indigenous to global drylands are known for adap- tation to pastoral environments and resilience to variations in cli- mate and shortages in resources (Ben Gara, 2000; Chedid et al., 2014). However, how much plasticity these breeds can express under accelerated trends of increased temperature, decreased pre- cipitation, and much higher frequency of extreme weather events is unpredictable. There are already signiﬁcant disruptions in water and feed availability and cyclicity, leading to mismatching with major events of the reproductive cycle of seasonal animals, includ- ing sheep (Kumar et al., 2017). Heat stress further disrupts animal physiology, depressing productivity and contributing to wider yield gaps (Rhind and McNeilly, 1986; Maurya et al., 2005; Pulina et al., 2007).
Sheep breeds with a shallow reproductive seasonality have their mating season starting in spring and through summer. This is typical of various Mediterranean and non-tropical dryland breeds, which tend to have moderate sensitivity to photoperiod changes, allowing them to time their main lambing season in autumn and the 1st months of winter (Rekik et al., 2005). To main- tain acceptable levels of reproductive performance following out- of-season mating, hormonal treatments and other techniques such as photoperiodism are widely used. Such interventions remain constrained by high cost, unavailability in many countries, and need for speciﬁc technical expertise. The ‘ram effect’ is an alterna- tive method for puberty induction and synchronisation of time of oestrus (Scaramuzzi and Martin, 2008). Its use in managing pub- erty and reproduction in yearling females is cost-effective, easily applied, and aligns with universal principles of human health (safe animal food sources without hormones), environmental health (less residues), and animal welfare (freedom to express normal behaviour). The ‘ram effect’ is commonly used, contributing to the success of reproduction out-of-season, in spring.
The implementation of the ‘ram effect’ is well-known, well-studied, and described in several countries, but continues to stimulate research because of complexity of the underlying neu- roendocrine mechanisms (Fabre-Nys et al., 2016). The major factor responsible for variability in the response of ewes to rams is ewes’ ‘depth of anoestrus’ (Marshall, 1903; Lindsay and Signoret, 1980; Oussaid et al., 1993). The Barbarine breed is a good representative of fat-tailed breeds in drylands. The traditional mating season is spring, during which 25-40% of adult ewes ovulate and exhibit oestrus, while the natural breeding season - when most ewes are sexually active - is mid-July to late February (Khaldi, 1989; Lassoued and Khaldi, 1995) (Fig. S1). Several papers have assessed the Barbarine response to the ‘ram effect’ (Khaldi, 1988; Lassoued and Khaldi, 1990) in an attempt to understand the underlying physiological mechanisms (Lassoued et al., 1997; Lassoued, 1998) and investigate its genetic mechanisms in adult, multiparous ewes (Maatoug-Ouzini et al., 2013). However, there is a gap concerning maiden ewes, representing 20-30% of flock composition and usu- ally with inherently lower reproductive performance than adults. Further to the large environmental effects on reproductive perfor- mance of maiden sheep, which need a more comprehensive assess- ment under a variable, erratic dryland ecosystem, genetics could greatly assist sheep holders in drylands to develop measures for adapting to global warming and climate change. However, accu- rately quantifying factors of variation requires large amounts of data. Therefore, this study investigated the response of Barbarine maiden ewes to the ‘ram effect’ under typical out-of-season man- agement of reproduction. We hypothesise that, over out-

Material and methods
Study location, animals and breeding practices
The data were collected over 26 years (1993-2016) by the Office de I’Elevage et des Paturages from its Jebibina-Saouef breed- ing farm located in Central Tunisia. The farm belongs to the Saouef subdistrict where the mean annual temperature is 18.1 °C and annual rainfall is 366 mm (Climate data.org, 2023). Temperature and precipitation were recorded here for 40 years, including the 26 years of the study period (Fig. 1). Long-term dynamics of Nor- malised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) were gathered from satellite missions Advanced Very High-Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR) (Fig. 1) and annual NDVI values were considered.
The animals were of the fat-tailed Barbarine breed (Atti and Bocquier, 1999; Ben Salem et al., 2011). The farm has nine Bar- barine ﬂocks, each comprising 250–300 ewes. The ﬂocks were housed outdoors year-round and grazed on natural and improved rangeland. In addition to grazing, the animals received supple- ments of hay (0.5–1 kg/head/day) and concentrates (200–300 g/h ead/day) during mating, late gestation, and beginning of lactation. Flocks were annually vaccinated against foot and mouth disease, brucellosis, and sheep pox and regularly received preventive antiparasitic treatments. Annually, breeding male lambs were selected at age 6 months on their growth performances using a Best Linear Predictor index. This index was also used for the selec- tion of replacement ewe lambs. Selected ewe lambs were kept as replacement and reared in complete isolation from rams starting from age 6 months postweaning. At age 18 months, immediately before they were ﬁrst mated, 40–50 of the maiden ewes were rein- troduced in each ﬂock. All ﬂocks were mated in spring every year, with rams introduced to all ﬂocks on the same day between 20 April and 10 May. On average, six rams were used for every 100 ewes, and ewes in all ﬂocks were totally isolated from rams for at least 6 weeks before joining. As a general practice, shepherd assistance is required to lift the tail at the time of copulation. This allows a full record of oestrus occurrences (twice a day) for each mating combination. As some rams can lift the fat tail without any help and mate and as in the studied farm, pedigree data are systematically recorded, the rams are usually separated from the females at night to prevent any uncontrolled mating events. All ewes were weighed prior to mating season, constantly exposed

Speciﬁcally, increased weight was associated with higher odds of Cyspon response. Thus, individuals of higher weight were more likely to exhibit Cyspon response than those of lower weight. Conversely, individuals of higher weight had a reduced likelihood of Cylate response than individuals of lower weight. However, weight did not signiﬁcantly impact the odds of Cynull response (Table 3).

Discussion
This study revealed that maiden Barbarine ewes were not totally sexually inactive during spring anoestrus months. Similar patterns were reported by De Lucas and Garcia (1991) for maiden Merino Rambouillet ewes in Mexico. However, comparisons should be considered cautiously because of age differences in what is des- ignated as nulliparous females. Capacity of sheep for out-of-season sexual activity was demonstrated in Barbarine (Tunisia; Maatoug- Ouzini et al., 2013), Mérinos d’Arles (France; Hanocq et al., 1999) and Chios ewes (Greece; Avdi et al., 2003) - these correspond to Mediterranean latitudes where the ‘ram effect’ proved an efficient management practice to trigger out-of-season female reproductive activity (Lassoued, 1998). In our study, spontaneous cyclicity (24%) and response to ‘ram effect’ of non—cyclic maiden ewes (50.45%) were lower than for multiparous Barbarine ewes (28 and 86%, respectively; Maatoug-Ouzini et al., 2013). Title: Climate smart breeding practices for sustainable sheep and goat production in pastoral systems
Description:
Enhancing sheep and goat productivity and returns from livestock enterprises in pastoral systems is vital to the communities whose livelihoods depend on their animals. However, realizing enhanced productivity and increased returns from small ruminant enterprises requires a combination of local livestock keepers’ knowledge, contemporary approaches to genetic improvement and husbandry that curtail Green house Gas emission and improve resilience alongside proactive market systems that facilitate diffusion of innovations and deliver value to value chain actors._x000D_

Title: Orientation training (Training of Trainers) for faculty members of Universities to deliver WEFE Nexus Gains Courses
Description: The orientation training(Training of Trainers) for faculty members of universities to deliver the new WEFE Nexus Course was organized from 9-10 April 2024 at Institute of Engineering (IoE), Tribhuvan University at Kathmandu Nepal.  The orientation training was based on the course designed in 2023 which included nexus concepts, principles, and tools to implement WEFE nexus approaches. The participants of the training included professors from Pakistan, Uzbekistan, and different regions of Nepal. The objective of the training was to enhance the theoretical understanding on nexus and to integrate the learnings into their courses and curricula. The training also provided the platform to discuss WEFE Nexus course contents, add regional perspective to it, and to revise the course accordingly.  It also supported strengthening WEFE nexus community of practice.
Evidence Parsed Text: The following text section comes from a specific evidence file named URL https://alliancebioversityciat.org/stories/training-tomorrow-leaders-integrated-sustainable-resource-management: "Blog Training Tomorrow s Leaders for Integrated and Sustainable Resource Management by Haley Zaremba, Marl ne Elias onOctober 15, 2024 Energy Gender, youth and inclusion Multifunctional landscapes Nepal Water New courses on water-energy-food-ecosystems (WEFE) nexus approaches aim to train natural resource managers to adopt integrated solutions to achieve sustainable, inclusive and resilient agri-food systems. The struggle to balance human and environmental wellbeing is becoming increasingly complex in an era of compounding global crises. Greater pressure on our shared resources in this changing context is creating new and wicked problems that will require new ways of problem-solving. To meet this challenge, the United Nations 17 interrelated Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) serve as a call to action for countries to work in global partnership to solve these complex issues. Working toward the SDGs requires unprecedented coordination and cooperation across borders and sectors. Although governments and practitioners typically manage food, water, and energy separately, these sectors are deeply interconnected and interdependent. As such, solutions and strategies for their sustainable development must also be interconnected to maximize synergies and mitigate trade-offs across sectors and stakeholders. To achieve this massive system shift, wide-scale capacity development is urgently needed. The next generation of water, energy, food, and ecosystem professionals must become water-energy-food-ecosystem (WEFE) nexus professionals, who think and work together in an integrated way to tackle wicked problems through nexus approaches. Cultivating the skills of tomorrow s nexus leaders To this end, the CGIAR Initiative on NEXUS Gains has supported the Center for Water Resources Studies (CWRS) from the Nepal Institute of Engineering at Tribhuvan University to create a new course series on WEFE nexus issues aimed at developing professional capacities for integrated, equitable, and sustainable resource management. These courses, which differ in format, target three distinct groups of current and future nexus professionals and policy/decision-makers: Sensitization course on the WEFE nexus for policy/decision-makers Professional course on the WEFE nexus for early to mid-career professionals Academic course on the WEFE nexus for graduate students Training tomorrow s leaders to employ nexus thinking and approaches is vital to enable these leaders to make informed decisions to optimize outputs from the available, limited resources. WEFE nexus training enables them to visualize interlinkages and interactions among WEFE resources while deciding on an intervention in a single sector, says Professor Vishnu Prasad Pandey, who led the development of the courses. In the spirit of a nexus approach, this course series was co-developed with professors and researchers from several different departments, fields of expertise, and research institutes, including CGIAR s Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT and International Water Management Institute (IWMI). This participatory and iterative process involved a series of multi-disciplinary workshops as well as piloting and revising the contents over three years in Nepal. Tribhuvan University will now be rolling out the resultant academic WEFE nexus course in two institutes central to resource management: Engineering and Forestry. Building momentum for nexus approaches worldwide Nepal is a forerunner in promoting WEFE nexus approaches for integrated resource management. The government is attempting to bring nexus thinking into some of its own resource ministries and policies, and the country s largest and most prominent university is taking a critical step to bring interdisciplinary nexus contents into its institutes. The CGIAR Initiative on NEXUS Gains is supporting global knowledge-sharing of the Nepal experience on nexus approaches. The course materials developed in Nepal are available with open access in the CGIAR NEXUS Gains resource repository to allow educators around the world to draw on this resource in their own teaching. Moreover, NEXUS Gains supported a Training of Trainers (ToT) in Kathmandu, held in April 2024, that brought together professors from Uzbekistan, Pakistan, and different regions of Nepal to discuss course materials and their effective delivery to aspiring nexus professionals. Led by Professor Pandey, the ToT, focused on nexus concepts, principles, and teaching strategies across the professional and educational contexts represented. The goal is that participants will bring nexus perspectives and ideas shared into their own courses and curricula. According to Professor Gulomjon Umirzakov, who participated in the ToT, The training provided invaluable insights into the interconnectedness of water, land, energy, forests, and biodiversity, and their crucial role in various aspects of life, including nutrition, health, food security, poverty reduction, and environmental sustainability. I am eager to share the insights gained from the training with my colleagues and faculty staff at the National University of Uzbekistan and to explore potential avenues for collaboration in advancing research and education in the field of the WEFE Nexus. Importantly, the ToT and the participatory process of developing the courses have contributed to building a network of knowledgeable nexus leaders and has helped to strengthen the foundation of a growing WEF(E) nexus Community of Practice. Future directions In the future, Professor Pandey calls for delivering professional nexus courses across the globe to create a critical mass of nexus practitioners in a global Community of Practice. Moving the needle to achieve more integrated approaches to WEFE management at scale will also require further engagement in policy spaces. We need to implement multiple iterations of the sensitization course for policy/decision makers in different countries to have the agenda of nexus-thinking internalized in policy/decision-making platforms at global level, says Pandey. The WEFE nexus course series is freely available here The course series and the associated Training of Trainers modules are supported by the CGIAR Initiative on NEXUS Gains and the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT. Title: The World’s First Seawater Irrigation Rice Salinity Screening Facility
Description: Developed the world's first salinity screening facility using the seawater irrigation. The rationale behind this is to mimic the farmers' real situation for more target-oriented sailnity tolerant varieties for coastal ecologies for Asia and ESA.  Set to transform rice climate resilience in saline ecosystems and identified 130  superior salinity-tolerant germplasm outperforming significantly better than the existing varieties.
Evidence Parsed Text:
The following text section comes from a specific evidence file named URL https://bit.ly/3SQiJiP: "Posted on Aug 14, 2024 Reinventing salt-tolerant rice breeding on ground zero Home News & Events News Dr. Hussain and his team established an innovative method of germplasm screening in a farmer's field at Infanta, a rice-growing municipality in the Philippine province of Quezon. (Photo: IRRI) Salinity is an agricultural problem that significantly affects rice production and is spreading in fields across the world. Poor irrigation practices, insufficient irrigation water during cropping seasons with low rainfall, high evaporation, increasing saline groundwater levels, and saltwater intrusion in coastal areas are among the significant causes of salinity. Salinity cuts rice production by 30 50%. Because this growing environmental crisis plagues the world's largest rice-producing and exporting countries, such as Vietnam, Thailand, Bangladesh, and India, it threatens the future of agri-food systems that feed billions of people. But millions of smallholder rice farmers living along the coastal areas of Asia and Africa are already feeling the brunt of this ever-spreading scourge. A vast and lasting damage Salinity inflicts long-lasting damage that affects generations of farmers. In October 1999, a tropical depression in the Andaman Sea gradually developed into a superstorm, the Paradip Cyclone, barrelling towards India. It became the most severe weather system to strike Odisha in the 20th century. For most, the damages caused by the cyclone are only a memory. The floods have receded, ruins have been rebuilt, and lives so violently interrupted have resumed. However, more than two decades later, rice farmers in the state's coastal region along the Bay of Bengal continue living with the cyclone's aftermath. Recently developed germplasm that exhibits tolerance to high-salinity levels using cutting-edge breeding techniques and a novel method of seawater irrigation for screening. (Photo: IRRI) Waseem Hussain, who leads the Global Rice Salinity and Flooding Breeding Program at the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI), visited the area recently and spoke with the rice farmers. "They told us that they used to grow rice in every field before 1999," Dr. Hussain said. "But the cyclone converted their farms into salt lands, and they said that they could not grow anything since. The salinity level goes very high during the dry season because it doesn't rain here." De-salting the earth There are several ways to manage salinity in the soil, but most are costly and beyond the reach of poor rice farmers. Developing salt-tolerant crop varieties is the most economical solution because it entails less resource use and is both practical and socially acceptable. Rice is more susceptible to salinity than other crops, and breeders worldwide have been working to develop varieties that can grow in afflicted soils. IRRI has accomplished much in this regard over the past 40 years, and various countries have released salt-tolerant rice varieties originating from IRRI's germplasm. Genetic history fails to repeat itself One of the most impactful milestones in rice breeding occurred in 1991 when researchers discovered the SUB1 gene from an unheralded Indian landrace designated FR13A (FR stands for "flood resistant"). The SUB1 gene, which enables rice to survive underwater for 14 days, has been introduced into several popular and high-yielding varieties for the millions of poor farmers in flood-prone areas worldwide that are rendered useless for rice production during the rainy season. In 2015, one of these varieties, Swarna-Sub1, was hailed as a significant innovation for helping rice farmers in flood-prone areas of India. The milestone gene for developing salt-tolerant rice is Saltol. The gene confers salinity tolerance, particularly during the seedling stage. Like SUB1, breeders have incorporated the Saltol gene into various rice varieties. However, a single gene like Saltol cannot provide a reasonable salinity tolerance and can grow in farmers' fields like SUB1 varieties. "We sent salt-tolerant germplasm materials to Bangladesh and India for testing," Dr. Hussain said. "In 2021, I visited some of the sites on farmers' fields in Bangladesh to see how the materials are performing. To my surprise, all of the materials were completely dead. None survived. I went to the other location, and the same thing happened. They were supposed to be salt-tolerant but didn't survive under those conditions in coastal belts. " One thing that caught Dr Hussain's attention during his visit to Odisha was the rice plants growing in small pockets. But they were farmers' landraces. He asked the farmers about the released varieties by public institutes. They said they don't grow or survive here, or if they grew, they produced very low yields. "It was pretty shocking to hear this from the farmers," Dr. Hussain said. "If we continue breeding salt-tolerant rice in the same manner we have been doing for the past 40 years, we will have the same story." Manufactured stress vs. real-world stress IRRI researchers developed screening techniques for rice salt tolerance conducted in a phytotron, a type of greenhouse where the temperature and relative humidity can be manipulated to minimize environmental interactions. The plants are screened at the seedling, vegetative, and reproductive stages. They are placed in styrofoam floats inside a plastic box containing a carefully formulated saline nutrient solution. The saline nutrient solution is carefully prepared, every ingredient precisely measured, and strictly maintained to ensure uniformity. Unlike the environment inside a phytotron, nature rules the real world. There are no knobs and switches to bend its forces to desired settings. IRRI breeders used artificial salts in salinity screening experiments under managed conditions. Artificial salts do not mimic the real condition of salinity stress in the farmer's field. "Conditions in farmers' fields are very dynamic and complex," Dr. Hussain explained. "The salinity level is highly unpredictable. Sometimes it will be low. Sometimes it will be high. When it rains, the level of salinity decreases. When it doesn't rain, the salinity level goes up. "Salinity can come at any time. It's not within the control of the farmers. It can happen at any stage of crop growth. Under experimental conditions, the plants are given very short treatment periods, for one or two weeks, and then evaluated to see how they responded." "An idea struck in my mind that to develop salt-tolerant rice varieties that can grow in these fields, we have to match the conditions in the fields," said Dr. Hussain. "Controlled or managed experiments do not reflect the true story of the farmers' fields." That's where Dr. Hussain and his team came up with the idea of establishing screening plots where the plants can experience the harsh realities of coastal environments. Ground zero for salt-tolerant rice breeding About 132 kilometers east of Manila, the Municipality of Infanta in Quezon Province, Philippines, is known for its traditional Filipino distilled palm liquor, lambanog. Its eastern border is coastal, touching Polilo Strait, and it has numerous seaside resorts. According to the Department of Agriculture, rice is cultivated in the municipality, where the average harvest is 2,932 kilograms per hectare. Infanta's climate rains throughout the year, with a pronounced rainy season from November to April. However, it is no stranger to natural calamities, particularly typhoons that form thousands of kilometers away in the heart of the Pacific Ocean. In 2004, Infanta suffered a fate similar to Odisha five years earlier. The town was heavily affected by four successive weather systems: two tropical depressions and two typhoons. These triggered flooding, landslides, and storm surges. Storm surges are the bane of coastal agricultural lands. Strong winds push seawater further inland, blighting the soil. The 2020 National Mapping, Characterization and Coastal Areas Affected by Salinity Development of Spatial Database for the Coastal Areas Affected by Salinity by the Bureau of Soils and Water Management reports that Infanta's coastal areas vary from non-saline to severely saline with more than 5,300 hectares exhibit moderately saline soil. From the perspective of salt-tolerant rice breeding, Infanta is ground zero. Dr. Hussain and his team set out to transform rice breeding using a radical approach that has never been done before. Reinventing conventional wisdom Although it seems counterintuitive, countless published scientific works using the standard screening protocol helped shape Dr. Hussain's revisionist approach to salt-tolerant rice breeding. He and his team reviewed the literature at IRRI and globally and found tremendous amounts of published research on various rice genes associated with salt tolerance. "Breeders have acquired an understanding of the biological mechanisms inside plants, Dr. Hussain said. "But whatever genes identified through ideal-conditions screening or greenhouse experiments have 0% translation in the field." So, Dr. Hussain and his team abandoned the established protocol of subjecting plants to short salinity periods and classified them as tolerant if they did not die. They set up the experimental site 200 meters from the coast, where seawater inundates the field during high tides. During low tides, they use a pump to draw water from the sea to irrigate the plants. Their inventive screening method subjected thousands of rice germplasm from previous breeding efforts at IRRI to salinity treatments not at a particular stage but throughout their life cycle up to the harvesting stage. "IRRI researchers have done a tremendous job of creating salt-tolerant germplasm from the International Rice Genebank," Dr. Hussain said. "I think that is our biggest advantage. The germplasm was already there. The only thing to do was to put them in real conditions and identify the best salinity-tolerant genotypes. It is like finding a needle in a haystack. A genotype refers to an organism s complete set of genes, which, in combination with environmental factors, determine its appearance and behavior. "It took us over three years to optimize their innovative screening experiment protocol in Infanta because it's not easy to do it in the field," he said. "But we have a very robust screening facility there now. When we want to identify salt-tolerant rice plants, we screen them in Infanta." Scientific heresy or the protocol of the future? This kind of out-of-the-box thinking made other breeders shake their heads in disbelief. Challenging any dogma will always elicit blowback and comes with a price for those with dissenting standpoints. But irrigating rice with seawater? "We were told our approach is very wrong," Dr. Hussain said. "We received much criticism from people telling us we cannot grow rice in the seawater because we will kill the plants. Rice is not halophyte (salt-tolerant), and it is impossible to grow rice in seawater. But our aim was not to grow the rice in seawater. We were trying to identify which genotype would respond with appropriate tolerance when we put them under real saline stress. We use the plants that endure in our breeding program to develop new varieties." The first lines the team identified and created new germplasm through crossing are in the testing stage of ongoing trials in India and Bangladesh. "I think they will perform," Dr Husain said. In three or four years, I expect suitable salt-tolerant varieties for coastal ecologies of Asia and Africa emanating from our newly identified germplasm at infanta. But the real test will begin in farmers' fields." Title: Ukama Ustawi field days: Increasing awareness and knowledge sharing on optimal livestock-crop production systems
Description: The CGIAR Initiative on Diversification in East and Southern Africa—Ukama Ustawi (UU)—recently convened two successful field days in Murehwa and Shamva districts in Zimbabwe, to promote livestock production in diversified maize-based agriculture systems managed under sustainable intensification. Organized by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and attended by around 100 farmers the field days not only provided an opportunity to showcase the work being done by farmers under the UU Initiative, but also opened channels for dialogue and reflection on the Initiative’s successes and lessons learnt.

Title: Presentation by a cassava geneticist at the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT) for the Rockefeller Foundation on the objectives, research efforts, and impact of the CIAT cassava breeding program
Description: The presentation provided an overview of the cassava breeding program at the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT), highlighting its key research areas and breeding pipelines. The program focuses on genetic improvement, trait selection, and the application of advanced breeding technologies to enhance cassava productivity and resilience. It also emphasizes the importance of partnerships with national agricultural research systems (NARS) to facilitate germplasm exchange and capacity building. Additionally, the program addresses challenges such as climate change and pest resistance, aiming to develop cassava varieties adaptable to various environmental conditions and meet the needs of smallholder farmers.

Title: Popularization of new climate resilient, high yielding and improved products through innovative and participatory extension methods organized in all key regions like Asia, Africa and Latin America
Description: A total of 234 (where IITA -03, IRRI Rice (Asia & Africa) -108, Wheat & Maize -100, ICARDA-05, and ICRISAT-18) promising products have been added to the seed chain. Many of the chosen varieties from the previous year's data were tested, positioned, and also scaled using a variety of innovative extension validation techniques and platforms. Popular strategies for raising awareness were participatory varietal cafeterias that involved a variety of stakeholders and conducted a thorough evaluation of the goods and attributes that patrons preferred. Simultaneously, community-led demonstration clusters made new varieties prominent and attracted the attention of influential people and key players in the seed chain for acceptance and scaling. Farmers, seed growers, dealers, and local extension agents of well-known agricultural development programs and schemes were all included in this.

Although many governments in the global South use seed subsidies to achieve these outcomes, the success and efficiency of input subsidies is subject to debate. Most smallholders in Nepal lack information and finance to access improved technologies, including improved seeds. To address this, Nepal's universal seed subsidy programme (SSP) began in 2012. SSP offers participants up to 50% off the price of rice seed from improved varieties. Purpose We evaluate the impact of SSP on farmer participants five years after its inception. Until now, the programme had not been evaluated. Approach and Methods We compare rice-growing households receiving subsidized seeds (treatment group) with those that do not (control group). We match the two groups using propensity scoring. We compare rice yield per hectare for the two groups, looking at aggregate and heterogeneous treatment effects. Primary data come from a 2019 survey of 157 treated and 173 control farm households in the Terai lowlands. Findings We find no evidence of SSP impact on rice yield in the aggregate. One potential explanation is that the programme tended to promote seed of a long-standing open-pollinated variety (OPV), rather than newer, higher-yielding OPVs and hybrids. Examination of heterogenous impacts, however, shows higher yields among treated households who were either on low incomes or remote from agro-dealers and agricultural extension offices. Policy implications Given the lack of impact on yields of SSP, sustaining the programme in the same form is neither advisable nor justified. We suggest targeting households on low incomes and in remote areas; subsidizing only the more recent high-yielding varieties; and considering cost-effective approaches to administer the programme, such as seed vouchers. To improve last-mile seed delivery, SSP needs to engage more with private seed providers and be more transparent in its operations. Results from this study may have broader implications for other long-standing agricultural subsidies in Nepal and other developing countries with universal subsidy programmes. 1 INTRODUCTION Agriculture remains the main driver of economic growth, food security, and poverty reduction in many developing countries in Asia and Africa (Thirtle et al., 2003; World Bank, 2008). The performance of agriculture in terms of farm productivity and food security has rapidly improved over the past few decades with wide adoption of technologies, including improved varieties and fertilizers (Fuglie et al., 2020; World Bank, 2007). However, many smallholder farmers in low-income countries still need to catch up in technology adoption (Evenson & Gollin, 2003; Pingali, 2012). Numerous factors hinder farmers' uptake of agricultural inputs in developing countries, such as input quality (Bold et al., 2015), affordability, access to financial services (Fuglie et al., 2020; Pingali, 2012), and ineffective extension and communication programmes (Druilhe & Barreiro-Hurl , 2012; Wiggins & Brooks, 2012). Developing countries have employed agricultural input subsidies to overcome these challenges despite economists' warnings about their potential for inefficiency, market distortions, and welfare losses (Schultz, 1964). Before the 1990s, many developing countries embraced universal subsidies, but these programmes proved costly and financially unsustainable. Several nations phased out subsidies between the 1960s and 1990s due to their failure to enhance productivity and food security, high and unsustainable costs, and skewed benefits toward larger farmers (Dorward, 2009; World Bank, 2007). However, multiple global economic crises, notably the 2007/2008 international food price crisis (Jayne et al., 2018), coupled with experimental evidence demonstrating the cost effectiveness of well-timed small-scale subsidies for improving technology adoption among farmers (Duflo et al., 2011), reignited interest and investment in agriculture among developing country policy-makers and donor partners (Dionne & Horowitz, 2016; Mason & Ricker-Gilbert, 2013; Morris et al., 2007; OECD, 2018; Rashid, Dorosh et al., 2013). Given the ongoing debate on the effectiveness of subsidies, there is growing interest among governments and donors to evaluate input subsidy programmes in developing countries, especially in Africa. Malawi stands out as a country where several studies have assessed the impact of a targeted Farm Input Subsidy Programme (FISP) introduced in 2005 2006 (Asfaw et al., 2017; Chibwana et al., 2012; Dorward & Chirwa, 2011; Fisher et al., 2014; Lunduka et al., 2013; Ricker-Gilbert et al., 2011). Fertilizer subsidies have also been evaluated in other African countries, such as Ethiopia (Rashid, Tefera et al., 2013), Tanzania (World Bank, 2014), and Zambia (World Bank, 2010). Input subsidies in Africa, mainly fertilizer subsidies, yield mixed and inconclusive results. Assessments of input subsidy programmes in sub-Saharan Africa show that targeted subsidies can enhance agricultural production and food security. However, their effectiveness hinges on managing challenges like transparent distribution systems, timely input availability, and addressing issues like leakages and fraud (Asfaw et al., 2017; Hemming et al., 2018; Wiggins & Brooks, 2012). Another strand of research on targeted agricultural subsidies in African nations highlights that these subsidies can discourage private sector involvement and investment in the agricultural input market, as subsidy inputs displace private sales, leading to market distortions and resource allocation effects (Mather & Jayne, 2018; Ricker-Gilbert et al., 2011). Unlike in Africa, where research on subsidies focuses on maize, rice (paddy) has been the focus in Asia. However, the number of studies in developing Asia is limited compared to Africa. In Sri Lanka, Ekanayake (2009) recommends a decades-long paddy fertilizer subsidy for gradual withdrawal due to its minimal impact on fertilizer use in paddy cultivation. In Southeast Asia, the reduction of price controls on production inputs like fertilizers and machinery is reported to contribute to the growth in rice production and motivate farmers to improve their productivity (Laiprakobsup, 2019). In Indonesia, fertilizer subsidies help paddy productivity but tend to favour larger farmers and lead to fertilizer overuse (Gomez Osorio et al., 2011). In India, input subsidies (fertilizer, irrigation, and credit) assisted small farmers during the early years of the Green Revolution; however, public investments in agricultural research, education, and rural roads proved more effective for agricultural growth and poverty reduction (Fan et al., 2007). Although substantial research examines fertilizer subsidies in developing countries, the body of evidence on the effectiveness of seed subsidies remains limited (Mason & Ricker-Gilbert, 2013). Seed subsidy impacts are often studied within broader input subsidy programmes, with only a handful focusing solely on seed subsidies (Druilhe & Barreiro-Hurl , 2012; Hemming et al., 2018), primarily maize seed subsidies in Africa. A randomized control trial of a seed subsidy voucher in Nigeria showed a significantly positive effect on household income and per capita consumption expenditure (Awotide et al., 2013). In Zambia, Mason and Smale (2013) estimated a modest positive impact of subsidized hybrid maize seed on total maize production, household income, and poverty severity. However, these results were sensitive to seed prices and administrative costs. In South Asia, evaluation of subsidies has been limited: what does exist focuses primarily on fertilizer subsidies, with some concerns raised about their fairness and transparency (Sinha, 2019). Few studies have evaluated impact of seed subsidies in South Asia. Use of seed subsidy showed a differential welfare effect for different income groups in Bhutan (Wang et al., 2019). Jaweriah and Mishra (2024) found positive effects of input subsidy card (subsidy package included seed) on rice yields and household income, especially among impoverished and smallholder Bangladeshi farmers. Bardhan and Mookherjee (2011) report positive yield impact of subsidized agricultural inputs in the form of mini-kits composed of seed (rice, oilseeds and potatoes), fertilizer and pesticide in India. Few studies have delved into equity within seed subsidy programmes. A study in Bhutan revealed that over 90% of surveyed households received some form of agricultural subsidy (Wang et al., 2019). However, wealthier households were more involved in improved cow breeds and biogas subsidies because they could cover higher co-payments. Conversely, lower-income farmers primarily participated in seed and sapling subsidy programmes. Agricultural machinery subsidies were observed to have counterproductive effects on low-income households. Our review of the literature reveals significant knowledge gaps in understanding the impact and effectiveness of agricultural subsidies, particularly in developing Asia compared to Africa. The existing literature suggests that the impact of subsidy programmes is not universal but context-specific, with some programmes showing profound positive economic, food security, and poverty impacts, while others yield negative impacts (Doward & Morrison, 2015; Jayne et al., 2018). For a robust and meaningful assessment, it is crucial to examine specific input subsidy programmes in a particular context and time. In Nepal, agricultural input subsidies are often reported misused and in some instances subsidy and grants programmes on agriculture development do not address the real issues of needy farmers (Shrestha, 2021), and politicians aim to avoid alienating this crucial electorate. Nevertheless, the Government of Nepal (GoN) acknowledges the lack of evidence regarding the effectiveness of agricultural subsidies. It recognizes the need for systematic reviews to enhance the impact of investments in agriculture (GoN, 2014). Similar political motivation for input subsidies is also observed in Africa. For instance, Mason and Ricker-Gilbert (2013) reported that in Malawi and Zambia constituencies where the ruling party had won the previous presidential election received more subsidies. The limited research that evaluates the impact and effectiveness of subsidies in Nepal has focused on fertilizer subsidies (Kyle et al., 2017; Paudel & Rago, 2017), whereas the effectiveness of seed subsidies remains largely unstudied. This study aims to address this knowledge gap by providing evidence on the impact of seed subsidies, elucidating farm-household implications, and offering policy-relevant recommendations. Our findings may inspire Nepalese policy-makers to evaluate the impacts of other agricultural subsidy components and support services. Beyond contributing to the existing literature on the impacts of agricultural subsidies, this study may offer insights for other developing countries, encouraging similar efforts to assess conventional input subsidy programmes and revise policies accordingly. 2 BACKGROUND Nepal increasingly relies on imported rice, maize, and wheat to meet its growing cereal demand, despite most Nepalese farmers focusing primarily on these crops. About 94% of the country's 3.7 million hectares of agricultural land is dedicated to cereal production, mainly rice, maize, and wheat. Agriculture in Nepal is predominantly composed of small subsistence farms, with an average landholding of 0.7 hectares and lower productivity than neighbouring countries in the region. Nepal's rice yield in 2013 was lower than the South Asian average: 3.17 mt/ha, compared to the regional average of 3.82 mt/ha (FAOSTAT, n.d.; MOALD, 2020). Despite marginal yield improvements in the past decade, Nepal's average rice yield in 2021 remained at 3.82 mt/ha, equivalent to the South Asian average in 2013. Historically, the Terai lowlands consistently achieved higher yields than the Hill region. In 2021, the Terai's average yield was 4.00 mt/ha, while the Hill region's average was 3.45 mt/ha. The national average yield in 2021 indicates a yield gap of 1.7 to 3.0 mt/ha compared to experimental yields (5.2 6.5 mt/ha) and a 1.0 to 1.5 mt/ha yield gap compared to attainable yields (4.5 5.0 mt/ha) (K.C et al., 2021). Nepal's cereal productivity is hampered by low fertilizer use and limited adoption of improved seeds (GoN, 2013; GoN, 2014). The government aims to double agricultural production in five years and recognizes that access to quality seeds is key to food security. GoN believes that improved seed varieties, with guaranteed quality, alone can boost yields by 20 30% (GoN, 2013, 2014). However, challenges in the rice grain and seed value chain raise serious doubts about achieving these targets. Choudhary, Khanal et al. (2022) analysed Nepal's rice seed supply and demand dynamics, linking the rice grain market to the seed value chain. They found that inconsistent paddy supply from domestic sources has resulted in most rice mills operating at just 50% capacity. As a result, urban demand for fine and aromatic rice relies heavily on imports. The limited availability of domestic fine and aromatic rice varieties contributes to this paddy shortfall. To address this gap, the GoN allowed the importation of five OPVs of fine rice in 2015. Furthermore, between 2017 and 2019, more than 41 new rice varieties were registered. Of these, only two were of domestic origin, the rest being imported varieties (Choudhary, Banskota et al., 2022). The registration of hybrids in Nepal began mainly in 2010, with approximately 17 hybrid rice varieties from India and China registered by 2014 (SQCC, 2014). Nepal currently has over 135 released and registered rice varieties, including hybrids from India and China, with nearly 60% introduced after 2000. In 2018, about 36% of households were found to cultivate hybrids, primarily for generating cash income, while the remaining 64% grew domestic OPVs, such as Sabitri, Radha-4, and Sawa Sub 1 (Choudhary, Khanal et al., 2022). In 2018, imported seeds accounted for 43.3% of Nepal's formal rice seed market, totalling 17,656 metric tons. Only 18% of these imports followed formal channels, while the majority, 82%, came through informal channels (Choudhary, Khanal et al., 2002). Among these informal imports, unregistered OPV seed comprised 80%. In addition, unregistered hybrid seeds also enter the country and are used primarily in Terai districts. In some years, their use has led to crop failures resulting from poor germination (Bhatta, 2019). The growing reliance on imported seeds exposes Nepalese farmers to vulnerability during disruptions, such as those experienced during the COVID-19 pandemic, which led to agricultural input shortages, including seeds (Gautam et al., 2023). Despite the significant potential of the rice seed sector in Nepal, challenges face the value chain (Gauchan, 2019). Local seed companies face hurdles when introducing new, competitive rice varieties to the market (Thapa et al., 2023). Agro-dealers, well established and widely recognized by farmers in different market segments in Nepal, have the potential to reach and educate many farmers and promote the adoption of new rice varieties (Gauchan et al., 2018; Subedi & Kattel, 2021). However, most cereal-growing households recycle their seeds for several years, reflected in the low seed-replacement rate (SRR) of major cereals below 23% (MoALD, 2020). Nepal, like many developing countries, has implemented agriculture input subsidies to promote the adoption of modern agricultural technologies, including fertilizer, improved seeds, and machinery. GoN introduced the seed subsidy programme (SSP) in 2011/12, which paved the way for its implementation as a national programme (Bista et al., 2018). The rollout of SSP was gradual, involving the recruitment of additional dealers, an expansion in geographic coverage, and increasing the quantity of seeds distributed through SSP. Initially, the programme started with limited subsidized seed sales in selected districts in 2011/12, temporarily halted sales in 2012/13, but resumed in 2013/14 (Thapa Magar et al., 2018). Over just four years, the volume of seeds distributed under SSP increased by a factor of 14, from 579 mt in 2011/12 to 7,826 mt in 2016/17, and the budget expanded by a factor of 24, from NPR 6.53 million in 2012 2013 to NPR 155.38 million in 20171 (Bista et al., 2018). National Seed Company Limited (NSCL),2 a government subsidiary, was entrusted with planning and executing SSP nationwide through its network of dealers, including co-operatives and private sector agrovets. SSP covered a range of crops, including major cereals, pulses, and oilseeds. However, its primary focus was on three OPV cereals: rice (mainly in the Terai region), wheat (primarily in the Terai region), and maize (primarily in the Hill region). SSP prioritized domestic non-hybrid varieties of these crops and aimed to boost crop yields by promoting high-yielding improved varieties among cereal farmers. NSCL plays a key role in SSP by sourcing improved seeds from its production units and procuring seeds from seed producer co-operatives and private sector seed companies through bidding. NSCL incurs various expenses, including collection, storage in NSCL warehouses, quality testing, packaging, and transport to its dealers, including private sector agrovets and co-operatives. These dealers offer farmers subsidized seeds and receive a margin for selling subsidized seeds. The SSP subsidy ranged from 25% to 50% of the market price of seeds, with maximum limits set at 2.6 hectares for farmers in the Terai region and 2.0 hectares per year for those in the Hills region. The guideline stipulated that subsidized seed prices should be at least 25% higher than the grain used for food. SSP directly subsidizes participants during purchases without using vouchers or coupons. In this sense, SSP ensures a consistent price for all participants within the area served by participating dealers without targeting specific households based on landholding size or socioeconomic characteristics. Furthermore, the government can redirect SSP resources to affected geographic areas during natural disasters such as droughts or floods. In such cases, improved seeds can be provided free of charge to affected farmers, as permitted by the allocated budget. The primary objective of SSP was to replace older seed varieties, encourage the use of quality assured seeds, and discourage reliance on informal sources or farmer-saved seeds. This initiative aimed to contribute to the GoN's efforts to enhance the seed-replacement rate and overall crop productivity. However, SSP faced criticism from private sector stakeholders who believed that it negatively affected the private seed industry by forcing them to compete with NSCL's subsidized prices. This is consistent with observations made in other countries (Morris et al., 2007). Concerns also emerged regarding NSCL's management, specifically regarding seed pricing, nationwide distribution, and potential malpractices (Maize seed purchase, 2019; Khatiwada, 2020). SSP's strong emphasis on the Terai, where private sector seed was more readily available, raised questions about fairness to hill farmers who found it less easy to access seeds (Thapa Magar et al., 2018). In 2018, GoN modified the implementation of SSP by authorizing District Agriculture Development Offices (DADOs) to oversee it. However, with the transition to federalism, DADOs were abolished, leading NSCL to resume its role in SSP (Thapa Magar et al., 2018). In many developing countries, political motivations often sustain agricultural subsidies without evidence of their effectiveness (Dionne & Horowitz, 2016; Mason & Ricker-Gilbert, 2013). Nepal has witnessed a substantial increase in subsidy spending over the years, but there remains a dearth of evidence as to their impact, particularly of seed subsidies. GoN's 20-year (2015 to 2035) Agricultural Development Strategy (ADS) advocates a more balanced approach to financing the agricultural sector. It emphasizes the reduction of subsidies and increased investments in agricultural research and extension (GoN, 2014). ADS recommends periodic reviews of agricultural subsidy programmes, ideally every five years. This study is timely because SSP completed its first five years of implementation in 2018. Nepal's transition to federal governance in 2015/16 led to the devolution of some agricultural extension programmes to provincial and local governments. However, these newly formed authorities have continued to provide seed subsidies without considering their effectiveness. This research represents the first empirical study to establish a causal link between SSP and its outcomes using a quasi-experimental approach. 3 METHODOLOGY 3.1 Conceptual framework This article evaluates the impact of the GoN's SSP using a case study of rice in two districts. Figure 1 illustrates the conceptual framework of the GoN's SSP. The objective of SSP is to increase access to improved seeds using price subsidies. The logic of SSP is that the subsidy will reduce costs for farmers and encourage the adoption of improved seed varieties to achieve higher yields (GoN, 2014). The realization of higher yields leads to improved farm income, which persuades farmers to continue using varieties promoted through subsidy programmes. The adoption of SSP-promoted varieties was already high, with 84% among control group households and 79% among treatment households in the base year (2013), indicating that most of the farmers sampled in both treatment and control groups were using SSP-promoted varieties before SSP started in the study area (Table A1 in the Appendix). In this regard, we look at yield rather than adoption as the SSP impact measure. We assume that the seed provided through SSP would be of better quality (purity, assured germination, and easier access) than seeds from other sources. In this sense, the treatment group (who received seeds from SSP) is expected to achieve a higher yield impact on average than the control group (which did not receive SSP seeds). The gain in yield is expected to have implications for food security and household income; however, it only makes sense to consider these higher-order outcomes when we find a conclusive significant treatment effect for yield. 3.2 Sampling and data collection This study was carried out in the adjoining districts of Banke and Bardia, in the western Terai of Nepal.3 We identified four villages to form a treatment cluster and four villages to form a comparison cluster. The selection of the villages was purposive. The villages were selected for the treatment group based on the highest number of seed subsidy recipients. For the control group, we identified some villages where SSP had not promoted subsidized seeds since it began in these two districts in 2013/14. We consulted several key informants (including co-operatives and agrovet managers) in treatment and control villages and NSCL officials in the region to narrow down to four villages most comparable to treatment villages, including proximity and similarities of farm households. NSCL dealers began seed distribution in certain villages in the study districts in the 2013/14 agricultural season, gradually expanding the number of villages covered and the quantity of seeds distributed in subsequent years. The treatment villages in our study received seeds through SSP in the 2014/15 season, while the control group did not receive any during the 2013 2018 period. As SSP was initiated in the two study districts in 2013/14, we consider 2013 the base year. We acquired a list of 1,342 non-repetitive households that received subsidized seeds from four purposively selected NSCL seed dealers (agrovets and co-operatives) who sold subsidized seeds between 2014/15 and 2016/17 rice seasons. This list was used as the sampling frame to draw a random sample of treatment households. We listed 1,500 households in four comparison villages from which we sampled control group households. Data collection took place in September 2019 over three weeks. For more details, see Table 1, which provides information on the villages included and sample sizes for the treatment and control groups. TABLE 1. (2022). 3.3 Econometric approach The major challenge in impact assessment is determining the counterfactual scenario, a hypothetical scenario that does not exist. In this regard, the most practical way to establish the causal effects of a subsidy programme would have been a randomized control design where households are assigned randomly to a treatment group and a control group. Then the average outcomes are compared between these two groups of households. The following equation would provide an unbiased estimate of impact: (1) where Ai represents the outcome variable of interest; Ti is a binary variable indicating if household i received or did not receive subsidized seed (1 = yes, i.e., treatment group, 0 = no, i.e., control group); Xi is a vector of household-level control variables; and i represents random and unobservable measurement error. However, agricultural subsidies, including the seed subsidy in Nepal, are not randomly assigned. Without such random assignment, evaluating subsidy programmes' causal effect on outcome indicators is challenging (Ricker-Gilbert et al., 2013). Without the random assignment of the subsidy, equation (1) yields an inconsistent and biased estimate of the programme impact (Lance et al., 2014). In such cases, it is customary to use quasi-experimental approaches like instrumental variables (IV) or propensity score matching (PSM) to control for selection bias and endogeneity (Khandker et al., 2010). Our survey data or other secondary data did not yield a suitable instrumental variable, so we resorted to PSM. PSM has been used to measure various impacts, including farmer training on the adoption of integrated pest management (IPM) practices in vegetable production in Bangladesh (Gautam et al., 2017); agricultural technology adoption on poverty in Bangladesh (Mendola, 2007); co-operatives on agricultural technology adoption in Ethiopia (Abebaw & Haile, 2013); improved maize varieties on poverty in Mexico (Becerril & Abdulai, 2010); and input subsidy programmes on yield and income in Kenya (Mason et al., 2016) and fertilizer subsidy on household food expenditure in Malawi (Chirwa, 2010), to name a few. PSM uses propensity scores based on observable household characteristics to construct a statistical comparison group. It forms a matched set of treated and untreated subjects with similar propensity score values. The probability of treatment assignment is conditional on observed covariates where the propensity score is a balancing score. For this method, conditional independence and the presence of common support are necessary assumptions (Khandker et al., 2010; Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983). It is possible to minimize such bias using statistical matching methods (Cochran & Rubin, 1973; Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983). In PSM, a score is estimated to compare households that participate in SSP (treatment group) with households that did not participate (control group) for the outcome variables of interest, and matched pairs are created using baseline characteristics. Abstract Purpose: The success factors of agricultural extension are not well known. In addition, extension services are often treated as homogeneous actors in agricultural research. We intend to show the impact of different strategies in agricultural extension. Methodology: A survey of 396 extension officers asking, for example, about the officer s strategies and the perceptions of their clients revealed important differences within the sample and explained both the strategies and their perceived success among farmers, according to a structural equation model. Findings: The analysis showed that extension officers who considered the knowledge of their clients to be good tended to focus on the environmental problems in agriculture and that this was taken up positively by their clients. A higher education of officers led to a stronger observance of farmers interests. Both the institutional environment and the sociodemographic factors also influenced the choice of strategies. Younger extension workers, for example, had a stronger environmental focus than older workers. Practical implications: A focus on environmental issues in agricultural extension seems to benefit farmers which indicates that more attention in extension should be given to ecological questions. Theoretical implications: These findings call for a thorough exploration of different agricultural extension strategies and their success. Originality: According to our knowledge, this is the first distinction between the success of different extension strategies. PMID: 38879711 PMCID: PMC11180187 DOI: 10.1038/s41598-024-64808-9 Item in Clipboard Display options Format Abstract Climate change has brought an alarming situation in the scarcity of fresh water for irrigation due to the present global water crisis, climate variability, drought, increasing demands of water from the industrial sectors, and contamination of water resources. Accurately evaluating the potential of future rice genotypes in large-scale, multi-environment experiments may be challenging. A key component of the accurate assessment is the examination of stability in growth contexts and genotype-environment interaction. Using a split-plot design with three replications, the study was carried out in nine locations with five genotypes under continuous flooding (CF) and alternate wet and dry (AWD) conditions. Utilizing the web-based warehouse inventory search tool (WIST), the water status was determined. To evaluate yield performance for stability and adaptability, AMMI and GGE biplots were used. The genotypes clearly reacted inversely to the various environments, and substantial interactions were identified. Out of all the environments, G3 (BRRI dhan29) had the greatest grain production, whereas G2 (Binadhan-8) had the lowest. The range between the greatest and lowest mean values of rice grain output (4.95 to 4.62 t ha-1) was consistent across five distinct rice genotypes. The genotype means varied from 5.03 to 4.73 t ha-1 depending on the environment. In AWD, all genotypes out performed in the CF system. With just a little interaction effect, the score was almost zero for several genotypes (E1, E2, E6, and E7 for the AWD technique, and E5, E6, E8, and E9 for the CF method) because they performed better in particular settings. The GGE biplot provided more evidence in support of the AMMI study results. The study's findings made it clear that the AMMI model provides a substantial amount of information when evaluating varietal performance across many environments. Out of the five accessions that were analyzed, one was found to be top-ranking by the multi-trait genotype ideotype distance index, meaning that it may be investigated for validation stability measures. The study's findings provide helpful information on the variety selection for the settings in which BRRI dhan47 and BRRI dhan29, respectively, performed effectively in AWD and CF systems. Plant breeders might use this knowledge to choose newer kinds and to design breeding initiatives. In conclusion, intermittent irrigation could be an effective adaptation technique for simultaneously saving water and mitigating GHG while maintaining high rice grain yields in rice cultivation systems.
