Although many governments in the global South use seed subsidies to achieve these outcomes, the success and efficiency of input subsidies is subject to debate. Most smallholders in Nepal lack information and finance to access improved technologies, including improved seeds. To address this, Nepal's universal seed subsidy programme (SSP) began in 2012. SSP offers participants up to 50% off the price of rice seed from improved varieties. Purpose We evaluate the impact of SSP on farmer participants five years after its inception. Until now, the programme had not been evaluated. Approach and Methods We compare rice-growing households receiving subsidized seeds (treatment group) with those that do not (control group). We match the two groups using propensity scoring. We compare rice yield per hectare for the two groups, looking at aggregate and heterogeneous treatment effects. Primary data come from a 2019 survey of 157 treated and 173 control farm households in the Terai lowlands. Findings We find no evidence of SSP impact on rice yield in the aggregate. One potential explanation is that the programme tended to promote seed of a long-standing open-pollinated variety (OPV), rather than newer, higher-yielding OPVs and hybrids. Examination of heterogenous impacts, however, shows higher yields among treated households who were either on low incomes or remote from agro-dealers and agricultural extension offices. Policy implications Given the lack of impact on yields of SSP, sustaining the programme in the same form is neither advisable nor justified. We suggest targeting households on low incomes and in remote areas; subsidizing only the more recent high-yielding varieties; and considering cost-effective approaches to administer the programme, such as seed vouchers. To improve last-mile seed delivery, SSP needs to engage more with private seed providers and be more transparent in its operations. Results from this study may have broader implications for other long-standing agricultural subsidies in Nepal and other developing countries with universal subsidy programmes. 1 INTRODUCTION Agriculture remains the main driver of economic growth, food security, and poverty reduction in many developing countries in Asia and Africa (Thirtle et al., 2003; World Bank, 2008). The performance of agriculture in terms of farm productivity and food security has rapidly improved over the past few decades with wide adoption of technologies, including improved varieties and fertilizers (Fuglie et al., 2020; World Bank, 2007). However, many smallholder farmers in low-income countries still need to catch up in technology adoption (Evenson & Gollin, 2003; Pingali, 2012). Numerous factors hinder farmers' uptake of agricultural inputs in developing countries, such as input quality (Bold et al., 2015), affordability, access to financial services (Fuglie et al., 2020; Pingali, 2012), and ineffective extension and communication programmes (Druilhe & Barreiro-Hurl , 2012; Wiggins & Brooks, 2012). Developing countries have employed agricultural input subsidies to overcome these challenges despite economists' warnings about their potential for inefficiency, market distortions, and welfare losses (Schultz, 1964). Before the 1990s, many developing countries embraced universal subsidies, but these programmes proved costly and financially unsustainable. Several nations phased out subsidies between the 1960s and 1990s due to their failure to enhance productivity and food security, high and unsustainable costs, and skewed benefits toward larger farmers (Dorward, 2009; World Bank, 2007). However, multiple global economic crises, notably the 2007/2008 international food price crisis (Jayne et al., 2018), coupled with experimental evidence demonstrating the cost effectiveness of well-timed small-scale subsidies for improving technology adoption among farmers (Duflo et al., 2011), reignited interest and investment in agriculture among developing country policy-makers and donor partners (Dionne & Horowitz, 2016; Mason & Ricker-Gilbert, 2013; Morris et al., 2007; OECD, 2018; Rashid, Dorosh et al., 2013). Given the ongoing debate on the effectiveness of subsidies, there is growing interest among governments and donors to evaluate input subsidy programmes in developing countries, especially in Africa. Malawi stands out as a country where several studies have assessed the impact of a targeted Farm Input Subsidy Programme (FISP) introduced in 2005 2006 (Asfaw et al., 2017; Chibwana et al., 2012; Dorward & Chirwa, 2011; Fisher et al., 2014; Lunduka et al., 2013; Ricker-Gilbert et al., 2011). Fertilizer subsidies have also been evaluated in other African countries, such as Ethiopia (Rashid, Tefera et al., 2013), Tanzania (World Bank, 2014), and Zambia (World Bank, 2010). Input subsidies in Africa, mainly fertilizer subsidies, yield mixed and inconclusive results. Assessments of input subsidy programmes in sub-Saharan Africa show that targeted subsidies can enhance agricultural production and food security. However, their effectiveness hinges on managing challenges like transparent distribution systems, timely input availability, and addressing issues like leakages and fraud (Asfaw et al., 2017; Hemming et al., 2018; Wiggins & Brooks, 2012). Another strand of research on targeted agricultural subsidies in African nations highlights that these subsidies can discourage private sector involvement and investment in the agricultural input market, as subsidy inputs displace private sales, leading to market distortions and resource allocation effects (Mather & Jayne, 2018; Ricker-Gilbert et al., 2011). Unlike in Africa, where research on subsidies focuses on maize, rice (paddy) has been the focus in Asia. However, the number of studies in developing Asia is limited compared to Africa. In Sri Lanka, Ekanayake (2009) recommends a decades-long paddy fertilizer subsidy for gradual withdrawal due to its minimal impact on fertilizer use in paddy cultivation. In Southeast Asia, the reduction of price controls on production inputs like fertilizers and machinery is reported to contribute to the growth in rice production and motivate farmers to improve their productivity (Laiprakobsup, 2019). In Indonesia, fertilizer subsidies help paddy productivity but tend to favour larger farmers and lead to fertilizer overuse (Gomez Osorio et al., 2011). In India, input subsidies (fertilizer, irrigation, and credit) assisted small farmers during the early years of the Green Revolution; however, public investments in agricultural research, education, and rural roads proved more effective for agricultural growth and poverty reduction (Fan et al., 2007). Although substantial research examines fertilizer subsidies in developing countries, the body of evidence on the effectiveness of seed subsidies remains limited (Mason & Ricker-Gilbert, 2013). Seed subsidy impacts are often studied within broader input subsidy programmes, with only a handful focusing solely on seed subsidies (Druilhe & Barreiro-Hurl , 2012; Hemming et al., 2018), primarily maize seed subsidies in Africa. A randomized control trial of a seed subsidy voucher in Nigeria showed a significantly positive effect on household income and per capita consumption expenditure (Awotide et al., 2013). In Zambia, Mason and Smale (2013) estimated a modest positive impact of subsidized hybrid maize seed on total maize production, household income, and poverty severity. However, these results were sensitive to seed prices and administrative costs. In South Asia, evaluation of subsidies has been limited: what does exist focuses primarily on fertilizer subsidies, with some concerns raised about their fairness and transparency (Sinha, 2019). Few studies have evaluated impact of seed subsidies in South Asia. Use of seed subsidy showed a differential welfare effect for different income groups in Bhutan (Wang et al., 2019). Jaweriah and Mishra (2024) found positive effects of input subsidy card (subsidy package included seed) on rice yields and household income, especially among impoverished and smallholder Bangladeshi farmers. Bardhan and Mookherjee (2011) report positive yield impact of subsidized agricultural inputs in the form of mini-kits composed of seed (rice, oilseeds and potatoes), fertilizer and pesticide in India. Few studies have delved into equity within seed subsidy programmes. A study in Bhutan revealed that over 90% of surveyed households received some form of agricultural subsidy (Wang et al., 2019). However, wealthier households were more involved in improved cow breeds and biogas subsidies because they could cover higher co-payments. Conversely, lower-income farmers primarily participated in seed and sapling subsidy programmes. Agricultural machinery subsidies were observed to have counterproductive effects on low-income households. Our review of the literature reveals significant knowledge gaps in understanding the impact and effectiveness of agricultural subsidies, particularly in developing Asia compared to Africa. The existing literature suggests that the impact of subsidy programmes is not universal but context-specific, with some programmes showing profound positive economic, food security, and poverty impacts, while others yield negative impacts (Doward & Morrison, 2015; Jayne et al., 2018). For a robust and meaningful assessment, it is crucial to examine specific input subsidy programmes in a particular context and time. In Nepal, agricultural input subsidies are often reported misused and in some instances subsidy and grants programmes on agriculture development do not address the real issues of needy farmers (Shrestha, 2021), and politicians aim to avoid alienating this crucial electorate. Nevertheless, the Government of Nepal (GoN) acknowledges the lack of evidence regarding the effectiveness of agricultural subsidies. It recognizes the need for systematic reviews to enhance the impact of investments in agriculture (GoN, 2014). Similar political motivation for input subsidies is also observed in Africa. For instance, Mason and Ricker-Gilbert (2013) reported that in Malawi and Zambia constituencies where the ruling party had won the previous presidential election received more subsidies. The limited research that evaluates the impact and effectiveness of subsidies in Nepal has focused on fertilizer subsidies (Kyle et al., 2017; Paudel & Rago, 2017), whereas the effectiveness of seed subsidies remains largely unstudied. This study aims to address this knowledge gap by providing evidence on the impact of seed subsidies, elucidating farm-household implications, and offering policy-relevant recommendations. Our findings may inspire Nepalese policy-makers to evaluate the impacts of other agricultural subsidy components and support services. Beyond contributing to the existing literature on the impacts of agricultural subsidies, this study may offer insights for other developing countries, encouraging similar efforts to assess conventional input subsidy programmes and revise policies accordingly. 2 BACKGROUND Nepal increasingly relies on imported rice, maize, and wheat to meet its growing cereal demand, despite most Nepalese farmers focusing primarily on these crops. About 94% of the country's 3.7 million hectares of agricultural land is dedicated to cereal production, mainly rice, maize, and wheat. Agriculture in Nepal is predominantly composed of small subsistence farms, with an average landholding of 0.7 hectares and lower productivity than neighbouring countries in the region. Nepal's rice yield in 2013 was lower than the South Asian average: 3.17 mt/ha, compared to the regional average of 3.82 mt/ha (FAOSTAT, n.d.; MOALD, 2020). Despite marginal yield improvements in the past decade, Nepal's average rice yield in 2021 remained at 3.82 mt/ha, equivalent to the South Asian average in 2013. Historically, the Terai lowlands consistently achieved higher yields than the Hill region. In 2021, the Terai's average yield was 4.00 mt/ha, while the Hill region's average was 3.45 mt/ha. The national average yield in 2021 indicates a yield gap of 1.7 to 3.0 mt/ha compared to experimental yields (5.2 6.5 mt/ha) and a 1.0 to 1.5 mt/ha yield gap compared to attainable yields (4.5 5.0 mt/ha) (K.C et al., 2021). Nepal's cereal productivity is hampered by low fertilizer use and limited adoption of improved seeds (GoN, 2013; GoN, 2014). The government aims to double agricultural production in five years and recognizes that access to quality seeds is key to food security. GoN believes that improved seed varieties, with guaranteed quality, alone can boost yields by 20 30% (GoN, 2013, 2014). However, challenges in the rice grain and seed value chain raise serious doubts about achieving these targets. Choudhary, Khanal et al. (2022) analysed Nepal's rice seed supply and demand dynamics, linking the rice grain market to the seed value chain. They found that inconsistent paddy supply from domestic sources has resulted in most rice mills operating at just 50% capacity. As a result, urban demand for fine and aromatic rice relies heavily on imports. The limited availability of domestic fine and aromatic rice varieties contributes to this paddy shortfall. To address this gap, the GoN allowed the importation of five OPVs of fine rice in 2015. Furthermore, between 2017 and 2019, more than 41 new rice varieties were registered. Of these, only two were of domestic origin, the rest being imported varieties (Choudhary, Banskota et al., 2022). The registration of hybrids in Nepal began mainly in 2010, with approximately 17 hybrid rice varieties from India and China registered by 2014 (SQCC, 2014). Nepal currently has over 135 released and registered rice varieties, including hybrids from India and China, with nearly 60% introduced after 2000. In 2018, about 36% of households were found to cultivate hybrids, primarily for generating cash income, while the remaining 64% grew domestic OPVs, such as Sabitri, Radha-4, and Sawa Sub 1 (Choudhary, Khanal et al., 2022). In 2018, imported seeds accounted for 43.3% of Nepal's formal rice seed market, totalling 17,656 metric tons. Only 18% of these imports followed formal channels, while the majority, 82%, came through informal channels (Choudhary, Khanal et al., 2002). Among these informal imports, unregistered OPV seed comprised 80%. In addition, unregistered hybrid seeds also enter the country and are used primarily in Terai districts. In some years, their use has led to crop failures resulting from poor germination (Bhatta, 2019). The growing reliance on imported seeds exposes Nepalese farmers to vulnerability during disruptions, such as those experienced during the COVID-19 pandemic, which led to agricultural input shortages, including seeds (Gautam et al., 2023). Despite the significant potential of the rice seed sector in Nepal, challenges face the value chain (Gauchan, 2019). Local seed companies face hurdles when introducing new, competitive rice varieties to the market (Thapa et al., 2023). Agro-dealers, well established and widely recognized by farmers in different market segments in Nepal, have the potential to reach and educate many farmers and promote the adoption of new rice varieties (Gauchan et al., 2018; Subedi & Kattel, 2021). However, most cereal-growing households recycle their seeds for several years, reflected in the low seed-replacement rate (SRR) of major cereals below 23% (MoALD, 2020). Nepal, like many developing countries, has implemented agriculture input subsidies to promote the adoption of modern agricultural technologies, including fertilizer, improved seeds, and machinery. GoN introduced the seed subsidy programme (SSP) in 2011/12, which paved the way for its implementation as a national programme (Bista et al., 2018). The rollout of SSP was gradual, involving the recruitment of additional dealers, an expansion in geographic coverage, and increasing the quantity of seeds distributed through SSP. Initially, the programme started with limited subsidized seed sales in selected districts in 2011/12, temporarily halted sales in 2012/13, but resumed in 2013/14 (Thapa Magar et al., 2018). Over just four years, the volume of seeds distributed under SSP increased by a factor of 14, from 579 mt in 2011/12 to 7,826 mt in 2016/17, and the budget expanded by a factor of 24, from NPR 6.53 million in 2012 2013 to NPR 155.38 million in 20171 (Bista et al., 2018). National Seed Company Limited (NSCL),2 a government subsidiary, was entrusted with planning and executing SSP nationwide through its network of dealers, including co-operatives and private sector agrovets. SSP covered a range of crops, including major cereals, pulses, and oilseeds. However, its primary focus was on three OPV cereals: rice (mainly in the Terai region), wheat (primarily in the Terai region), and maize (primarily in the Hill region). SSP prioritized domestic non-hybrid varieties of these crops and aimed to boost crop yields by promoting high-yielding improved varieties among cereal farmers. NSCL plays a key role in SSP by sourcing improved seeds from its production units and procuring seeds from seed producer co-operatives and private sector seed companies through bidding. NSCL incurs various expenses, including collection, storage in NSCL warehouses, quality testing, packaging, and transport to its dealers, including private sector agrovets and co-operatives. These dealers offer farmers subsidized seeds and receive a margin for selling subsidized seeds. The SSP subsidy ranged from 25% to 50% of the market price of seeds, with maximum limits set at 2.6 hectares for farmers in the Terai region and 2.0 hectares per year for those in the Hills region. The guideline stipulated that subsidized seed prices should be at least 25% higher than the grain used for food. SSP directly subsidizes participants during purchases without using vouchers or coupons. In this sense, SSP ensures a consistent price for all participants within the area served by participating dealers without targeting specific households based on landholding size or socioeconomic characteristics. Furthermore, the government can redirect SSP resources to affected geographic areas during natural disasters such as droughts or floods. In such cases, improved seeds can be provided free of charge to affected farmers, as permitted by the allocated budget. The primary objective of SSP was to replace older seed varieties, encourage the use of quality assured seeds, and discourage reliance on informal sources or farmer-saved seeds. This initiative aimed to contribute to the GoN's efforts to enhance the seed-replacement rate and overall crop productivity. However, SSP faced criticism from private sector stakeholders who believed that it negatively affected the private seed industry by forcing them to compete with NSCL's subsidized prices. This is consistent with observations made in other countries (Morris et al., 2007). Concerns also emerged regarding NSCL's management, specifically regarding seed pricing, nationwide distribution, and potential malpractices (Maize seed purchase, 2019; Khatiwada, 2020). SSP's strong emphasis on the Terai, where private sector seed was more readily available, raised questions about fairness to hill farmers who found it less easy to access seeds (Thapa Magar et al., 2018). In 2018, GoN modified the implementation of SSP by authorizing District Agriculture Development Offices (DADOs) to oversee it. However, with the transition to federalism, DADOs were abolished, leading NSCL to resume its role in SSP (Thapa Magar et al., 2018). In many developing countries, political motivations often sustain agricultural subsidies without evidence of their effectiveness (Dionne & Horowitz, 2016; Mason & Ricker-Gilbert, 2013). Nepal has witnessed a substantial increase in subsidy spending over the years, but there remains a dearth of evidence as to their impact, particularly of seed subsidies. GoN's 20-year (2015 to 2035) Agricultural Development Strategy (ADS) advocates a more balanced approach to financing the agricultural sector. It emphasizes the reduction of subsidies and increased investments in agricultural research and extension (GoN, 2014). ADS recommends periodic reviews of agricultural subsidy programmes, ideally every five years. This study is timely because SSP completed its first five years of implementation in 2018. Nepal's transition to federal governance in 2015/16 led to the devolution of some agricultural extension programmes to provincial and local governments. However, these newly formed authorities have continued to provide seed subsidies without considering their effectiveness. This research represents the first empirical study to establish a causal link between SSP and its outcomes using a quasi-experimental approach. 3 METHODOLOGY 3.1 Conceptual framework This article evaluates the impact of the GoN's SSP using a case study of rice in two districts. Figure 1 illustrates the conceptual framework of the GoN's SSP. The objective of SSP is to increase access to improved seeds using price subsidies. The logic of SSP is that the subsidy will reduce costs for farmers and encourage the adoption of improved seed varieties to achieve higher yields (GoN, 2014). The realization of higher yields leads to improved farm income, which persuades farmers to continue using varieties promoted through subsidy programmes. The adoption of SSP-promoted varieties was already high, with 84% among control group households and 79% among treatment households in the base year (2013), indicating that most of the farmers sampled in both treatment and control groups were using SSP-promoted varieties before SSP started in the study area (Table A1 in the Appendix). In this regard, we look at yield rather than adoption as the SSP impact measure. We assume that the seed provided through SSP would be of better quality (purity, assured germination, and easier access) than seeds from other sources. In this sense, the treatment group (who received seeds from SSP) is expected to achieve a higher yield impact on average than the control group (which did not receive SSP seeds). The gain in yield is expected to have implications for food security and household income; however, it only makes sense to consider these higher-order outcomes when we find a conclusive significant treatment effect for yield. 3.2 Sampling and data collection This study was carried out in the adjoining districts of Banke and Bardia, in the western Terai of Nepal.3 We identified four villages to form a treatment cluster and four villages to form a comparison cluster. The selection of the villages was purposive. The villages were selected for the treatment group based on the highest number of seed subsidy recipients. For the control group, we identified some villages where SSP had not promoted subsidized seeds since it began in these two districts in 2013/14. We consulted several key informants (including co-operatives and agrovet managers) in treatment and control villages and NSCL officials in the region to narrow down to four villages most comparable to treatment villages, including proximity and similarities of farm households. NSCL dealers began seed distribution in certain villages in the study districts in the 2013/14 agricultural season, gradually expanding the number of villages covered and the quantity of seeds distributed in subsequent years. The treatment villages in our study received seeds through SSP in the 2014/15 season, while the control group did not receive any during the 2013 2018 period. As SSP was initiated in the two study districts in 2013/14, we consider 2013 the base year. We acquired a list of 1,342 non-repetitive households that received subsidized seeds from four purposively selected NSCL seed dealers (agrovets and co-operatives) who sold subsidized seeds between 2014/15 and 2016/17 rice seasons. This list was used as the sampling frame to draw a random sample of treatment households. We listed 1,500 households in four comparison villages from which we sampled control group households. Data collection took place in September 2019 over three weeks. In this regard, the most practical way to establish the causal effects of a subsidy programme would have been a randomized control design where households are assigned randomly to a treatment group and a control group. Then the average outcomes are compared between these two groups of households. However, agricultural subsidies, including the seed subsidy in Nepal, are not randomly assigned. Without such random assignment, evaluating subsidy programmes' causal effect on outcome indicators is challenging (Ricker-Gilbert et al., 2013). Without the random assignment of the subsidy, equation (1) yields an inconsistent and biased estimate of the programme impact (Lance et al., 2014). In such cases, it is customary to use quasi-experimental approaches like instrumental variables (IV) or propensity score matching (PSM) to control for selection bias and endogeneity (Khandker et al., 2010). Our survey data or other secondary data did not yield a suitable instrumental variable, so we resorted to PSM. PSM has been used to measure various impacts, including farmer training on the adoption of integrated pest management (IPM) practices in vegetable production in Bangladesh (Gautam et al., 2017); agricultural technology adoption on poverty in Bangladesh (Mendola, 2007); co-operatives on agricultural technology adoption in Ethiopia (Abebaw & Haile, 2013); improved maize varieties on poverty in Mexico (Becerril & Abdulai, 2010); and input subsidy programmes on yield and income in Kenya (Mason et al., 2016) and fertilizer subsidy on household food expenditure in Malawi (Chirwa, 2010), to name a few. PSM uses propensity scores based on observable household characteristics to construct a statistical comparison group. It forms a matched set of treated and untreated subjects with similar propensity score values. The probability of treatment assignment is conditional on observed covariates where the propensity score is a balancing score. For this method, conditional independence and the presence of common support are necessary assumptions (Khandker et al., 2010; Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983). It is possible to minimize such bias using statistical matching methods (Cochran & Rubin, 1973; Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983). In PSM, a score is estimated to compare households that participate in SSP (treatment group) with households that did not participate (control group) for the outcome variables of interest, and matched pairs are created using baseline characteristics. Abstract Purpose: The success factors of agricultural extension are not well known. In addition, extension services are often treated as homogeneous actors in agricultural research. We intend to show the impact of different strategies in agricultural extension. Methodology: A survey of 396 extension officers asking, for example, about the officer s strategies and the perceptions of their clients revealed important differences within the sample and explained both the strategies and their perceived success among farmers, according to a structural equation model. Findings: The analysis showed that extension officers who considered the knowledge of their clients to be good tended to focus on the environmental problems in agriculture and that this was taken up positively by their clients. A higher education of officers led to a stronger observance of farmers interests. Both the institutional environment and the sociodemographic factors also influenced the choice of strategies. Younger extension workers, for example, had a stronger environmental focus than older workers. Practical implications: A focus on environmental issues in agricultural extension seems to benefit farmers which indicates that more attention in extension should be given to ecological questions. Theoretical implications: These findings call for a thorough exploration of different agricultural extension strategies and their success. Originality: According to our knowledge, this is the first distinction between the success of different extension strategies. PMID: 38879711 PMCID: PMC11180187 DOI: 10.1038/s41598-024-64808-9 Item in Clipboard Display options Format Abstract Climate change has brought an alarming situation in the scarcity of fresh water for irrigation due to the present global water crisis, climate variability, drought, increasing demands of water from the industrial sectors, and contamination of water resources. Accurately evaluating the potential of future rice genotypes in large-scale, multi-environment experiments may be challenging. A key component of the accurate assessment is the examination of stability in growth contexts and genotype-environment interaction. Using a split-plot design with three replications, the study was carried out in nine locations with five genotypes under continuous flooding (CF) and alternate wet and dry (AWD) conditions. Utilizing the web-based warehouse inventory search tool (WIST), the water status was determined. To evaluate yield performance for stability and adaptability, AMMI and GGE biplots were used. The genotypes clearly reacted inversely to the various environments, and substantial interactions were identified. Out of all the environments, G3 (BRRI dhan29) had the greatest grain production, whereas G2 (Binadhan-8) had the lowest. The range between the greatest and lowest mean values of rice grain output (4.95 to 4.62 t ha-1) was consistent across five distinct rice genotypes. The genotype means varied from 5.03 to 4.73 t ha-1 depending on the environment. In AWD, all genotypes out performed in the CF system. With just a little interaction effect, the score was almost zero for several genotypes (E1, E2, E6, and E7 for the AWD technique, and E5, E6, E8, and E9 for the CF method) because they performed better in particular settings. The GGE biplot provided more evidence in support of the AMMI study results. The study's findings made it clear that the AMMI model provides a substantial amount of information when evaluating varietal performance across many environments. Out of the five accessions that were analyzed, one was found to be top-ranking by the multi-trait genotype ideotype distance index, meaning that it may be investigated for validation stability measures. The study's findings provide helpful information on the variety selection for the settings in which BRRI dhan47 and BRRI dhan29, respectively, performed effectively in AWD and CF systems. Plant breeders might use this knowledge to choose newer kinds and to design breeding initiatives. In conclusion, intermittent irrigation could be an effective adaptation technique for simultaneously saving water and mitigating GHG while maintaining high rice grain yields in rice cultivation systems. Rice is the mainstay of agriculture in Assam, said Mowsam Hazarika, Director of the Assam Seed and Organic Seed Certification Agency. Rice is grown in 2.4 million hectares, out of the 2.6 million hectares under food grains in the state, producing 5.2 million tons of grain. In 2020 2022, rice production contributed 5.5 million tons or 95% of the total food grains in Assam. However, the average productivity of rice in the state is only 2.2 tons/hectare, which is lower than the national average of 2.7 t/ha, according to Mr. Hazarika. Unavailability and non-accessibility to quality seed is a persisting problem in the region, he added. Most of the public- and private-sector seed companies have little or no presence in Assam. Only a few individual seed entrepreneurs and private seed companies are actively engaged in paddy seed production in Assam that contribute to the seed system. In 2023-2024, 19% of the total seed production area is registered to 33 farmer-producer companies and Assam Seed Corporation Ltd. The remaining areas are registered to individual seed entrepreneurs and private seed farms. IRRI South Asia Seed Systems and Product Management Lead and 2023 Borlaug Field Awardee Dr. Swati Nayak cited examples of different successful models of seed business across different countries. Dr. Nayak encouraged seed entrepreneurs to map the demand and supply of different paddy varieties in Assam. During the activity, participants developed a roadmap where public and private seed companies can work together to address the challenges of the seed business in Assam. through a better convergence platform."

The following text section comes from a specific evidence file named URL https://ricetoday.irri.org/variety-based-climate-smart-intervention-helps-smallholder-farmers-cope-with-flood-in-the-lowlands-of-odisha/: "Variety-based climate-smart intervention helps smallholder farmers cope with floods in the lowlands of Odisha September 5, 2023 by Mosharaf Hossain, Swati Nayak, Girija Swain, Pavan Yeggina, and Mukund Variar Natural calamities, primarily floods, of varying intensity adversely affect the standing crop leading to poor harvests. Such untoward climatic shocks invariably hit almost all blocks of Puri District in Odisha. The variety-based climate-smart intervention proved to be a potential response in the flood-prone rice areas. This can be replicated and scaled up in other blocks within the district as part of contingency plans for rice-growing areas affected by floods in the state. Agriculture in Odisha, India added 20.6% to the Gross State Value in 2021-22 with the low-land coastal district of Puri as one of the major contributors, according to the Odisha Economic Survey. Topographically, 58% of the 0.189 million hectares of cultivated land in this geography are classified as shallow and deep lowlands, and the remaining is medium land. Rice, oilseeds, green and black grams, and vegetables (eggplant, potato, okra, cauliflower, and tomato) are the major crops grown during the wet and dry seasons. With a high irrigation coverage of 70% (from canals), the district has an impressive cropping intensity of 217%. Rice is the primary crop grown in the wet season and is planted on approximately 94,000 hectares mostly in the lowlands (88% of the total winter rice area). Despite the high irrigation coverage and the high proportion of fertile alluvial soils in more than half of the area favorable for rice cultivation, production, and productivity are seriously challenged by recurring floods (August to September), salinity (February to March), drought (mid-July), and occasional cyclonic storms (September to November). These natural calamities, primarily floods, of varying intensity adversely affect the standing crop leading to poor harvests. Such untoward climatic shocks invariably hit almost all blocks of Puri. The impact of the frequent flood crisis The southwest monsoon in the district normally sets in around the third week of June and withdraws in the last week of September. It brings an average of 1,061 mm of rainfall, which is 82% of the yearly precipitation. Based on this climatic norm and meteorological forecast, farmers normally transplant rice towards the end of July to mid-August. In 2022, heavy monsoon rains in early and mid-August, caused by a weather system over the Bay of Bengal, triggered several distributaries of the Mahanadi River to overflow and inundate vast tracts of newly transplanted rice areas in the district. Nimapara was among the areas where farmers suffered significant crop losses because of prolonged flooding. The Dhanua River that passes through Nimapada floods the villages of Kothakusang, Balange, and Bamanal for 15-25 days, depending upon soil topography and water drainage efficiency. The GIS Laboratory at the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) mapped the flooded tract in the district and estimated the affected area. Pre- (06 August) and post- (18 August) flood sentinel-1 SAR images corroborated the occurrence of high-intensity floods and detected a large impacted area. GIS-based estimation indicated that, in Nimapada alone, the flood affected 3,739 hectares of rice fields. Spatial flood inundation maps generated for Nimapara showed large rice areas under water. An estimated 12,563 ha rice area spread across blocks of Gop, Astaranga, Kaktapur, Nimapada, and Pipli were flooded for at least 10 days. Recommended contingency plan for the flood crisis In such a worst-case scenario, farmers need coping mechanisms to salvage crops and minimize seasonal crop losses. Plant flood-tolerant rice varieties. Farmers in the village planted high-yielding rice varieties including Swarna, Sarala, CR dhan-1018, among others that are prone to submergence. Thus, flood-induced crop damage could not be averted. Farmers in flood-prone lowland areas should plant long-duration (140-150 days) flood-tolerant rice varieties. Two established flood-tolerant rice varieties, CR 1009-Sub1, and Swarna-Sub1, can offset the impact of crop inundation and ensure a reasonable harvest. Although flood-tolerant rice varieties would have been a better choice, even these could fail if floodwaters remain stagnant for more than 15 days. Stagnant flood (SF) tolerance is needed but there are no known rice varieties that combine flood and SF tolerance that can withstand both flash and stagnant floods. Replant flood-damaged fields. After the flood water recedes, farmers can replant their fields with rice seedlings secured from other places to replace their damaged crops. However, not every farmer can afford and arrange for seedlings given the short period. Oftentimes, seedlings in nearby areas are hardly available. Even if they are, rice seedlings are often too old and no longer suitable for transplanting. Such challenges, along with logistical bottlenecks and increased production costs, deter farmers from replanting their flood-damaged lands. After suffering from crop losses in August, there is a small window for growing suitable early maturing rice varieties as a post-flood crop. If the post-flood field is managed agronomically, and farmers replant an early maturing variety (100-110 days) preferably using the wet direct-seeded rice (DSR) method, a reasonable yield is fairly assured. This is a better proposition than losing the entire crop and the land being fallow thereafter. Farmers usually hesitate to adopt the first two recommendations because of a lack of awareness about flood-tolerant varieties or the availability of seedlings for replanting. However, the third option could be operationally easier and more financially rewarding, But this coping mechanism have not been fully tested and promoted under the said conditions. A variety-based climate-smart intervention With its considerable research base in Odisha, IRRI curated a technical fix to address the impact of the climatic crisis. In association with Pragati Koraput, a non-government organization in Odisha, IRRI introduced variety-based intervention in four flood-affected villages in Nimapada in the first week of September. The intervention included 55 affected farmers covering 25 hectares of rice areas identified using data, GIS-enabled mapping, and field observations. Two early maturing varieties, CR dhan-101 (Ankit) and CR dhan-102 (Santabhima), were chosen based on their performance in earlier varietal evaluation programs conducted by the IRRI Seed System. These two varieties mature in 105-110 days, have an average yield of 4 tons/ha, and are moderately resistant to major diseases and pests. Because the maturity of these varieties fits within the short time window (September to December) for growing crops, these short-duration varieties could replace the yield of the late-maturing varieties lost to flooding. Field observations and learning To demonstrate the variety-based intervention, IRRI held several meetings and orientations to create awareness among the participating farmers. The IRRI Team encouraged farmers to sow the varieties using the wet DSR method in areas where drainage was feasible instead of traditional transplanting. The team also issued and shared recommended nutrient management advisories for the altered field ecology. The IRRI Team closely monitored the seed sowing, nutrient management practices, and the different phases of crop growth. Several post-flood rice plots that were fallowed after the flood damage served as the ideal control plot for assessing the intervention impact. During the interaction between IRRI scientists and participating farmers, it was determined that only a few farmers could manage to acquire some seedlings from other villages to replant and harvest a moderate crop. Those who did not have that option were forced to keep their land fallow. As a result, large swathes of land were uncultivated following the flood. How the variety-based intervention could help farmers The farmers under the intervention, however, have a reason to smile. The early maturing varieties flourished and yielded at least 3.5 tons/ha. The good productivity of the recommended varieties could help farmers make up for the losses due to floods. Even if farmers suffer from crop damage due to flooding in September, they could still grow the recommended rice varieties and have a respectable harvest. Thus, the varieties could act as stand-by crops that farmers can sow, rather than fallowing, if the first late-maturing variety succumbs to floods My land was about to lie vacant this season after the flood, said Mr.Bijay Kumar Singh a farmer who was part of the program. But with Ankit, I harvested a decent yield comparable to the damaged and lost yield of Swarna and CR-1009. The recommended varieties matured in time (mid-December) enabling the field to be free for the farmers to sow the next crops mostly summer rice, green gram, and vegetables. Other local farmers stated that these varieties could potentially alter the lives of hundreds of small and marginal farmers with limited resources. Wet-DSR was a suggested option but farmers preferred to opt to raise nurseries and transplant early, reducing the risk of losing the crop due to further flooding. Rice as a contingency crop Because of the low-lying land in the region, early-maturing varieties are not best-fit options under normal scenarios; hence farmers were not aware of these varieties. Raising awareness of these varieties through this intervention empowers farmers to formulate a crop contingency plan for the next season. Almost all the participating farmers will keep some seeds of these varieties as part of a contingency plan next year, said Mr. Ramesh Chandra Mangaraj, another program participant who immensely benefited from the intervention. The variety-based intervention proved to be a pertinent and potential response in flood-prone rice areas. This can be replicated and scaled up in other blocks within the district and beyond. IRRI will share such evidence-backed experience with district and state agriculture departments as it can be suitably included in a contingency plan for flood-affected rice growing areas in the state. With the learning and insights from these field-based interventions, IRRI will facilitate need-based targeting of the area in 2024 and emphasize building farmers capacity to better manage flood-related farm losses. IRRI will also support agencies and machinery to boost the popularity and significance of specific varieties through other innovative extension methods. Engagement with important seed system stakeholders can further disseminate these varieties and amplify seed production. IRRI will further diffuse this response with the grassroots-level organizations in the region that worked with IRRI, directly or indirectly. To take on complex problems, solutions need to be fostered and advanced collectively by all key stakeholders to best serve farmers interests. These new varieties, which were evaluated through participatory rice variety evaluation through varietal cafeteria conducted by the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) and the Nepal Agricultural Research Council (NARC), offer the potential to address Nepal's growing food security needs. The varietal cafeterias were conducted in two locations Khajura, Banke District in the Western Region, and Belchapi, Dhanusha District in the Central Region on 20 October and 30 October 2023, respectively. A total of 23 rice varieties were evaluated, including three recently released varieties (Hardinath-4, Hardinath-5, and Hardinath-6), 18 potential pipeline varieties, and two local checks (Sarju-52 and Sona Mansuli). Participants at the field days, which were attended by farmers and other stakeholders such as extension agents, researchers, seed entrepreneurs, and seed companies, evaluated the varieties based on various agronomic traits, including yield, growth duration, grain quality, and disease resistance. Results of the participatory varietal evaluation trials revealed that several promising new varieties emerged, with Hardinath-6, BRRI Dhan 72, IR18R1119, BRRI Dhan 74, and Hardinath-5 being identified as the top five best-performing varieties in the Western Region. In the Central Region, the top five best-performing varieties were Hardinath-6, BRRI Dhan 72, Hardinath-5, Hardinath-4, and Sona Mansuli. These results suggest that these varieties have the potential to thrive in the diverse agro-ecological conditions of Nepal. The identification of these promising new rice varieties marks a significant step forward in Nepal's efforts to enhance rice productivity and food security. The promotion of these varieties through sustainable local seed systems will ensure that farmers have timely access to quality seeds, enabling them to maximize their crop yields and improve their livelihoods. IRRI and NARC are committed to supporting the further development and promotion of these promising new rice varieties. These efforts will contribute to Nepal's goal of achieving rice self-sufficiency and ensuring food security for its growing population. ### Learn more about IRRI (www.irri.org) or follow us on social media and networks (all links down the right column). Currently, the region is facing a 40% fodder deficit. Dr Stanford Blade, Deputy Director General-Research of ICRISAT, highlighted the collaborative nature of the project. This initiative reflects ICRISAT s commitment to delivering demand-driven innovations. Partnering with SKUAST has allowed us to co-develop sustainable solutions that benefit smallholder farmers and the broader agricultural sector, said Dr Blade. Article 27 June 2019 Use our pre-submission checklist Avoid common mistakes on your manuscript. 1 Introduction One of the most significant food crops is rice, which is directly eaten by almost half of the world's population [ 1 ]. It is followed in importance by maize and wheat. Each year, 162 million ha of rice are harvested and 85% of the entire production of rice is used for human consumption [ 2 ]. More than 100 nations cultivate rice, with Asia accounting for 90% of worldwide output. Even though there are over 110,000 varieties of rice that are grown, each with a distinct nutritional composition and quality, rice can only be categorized as either white or brown after post-harvest processing [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ]. About 21% of the worldwide human population's calories and 15% of their protein comes from rice [ 7 ]. Rice protein has a good nutritional quality rating among cereals and it also contains fiber, vitamins, and minerals [ 8 ]. The nutritional composition of rice is not the only determinant of its quality; other criteria that are essential for consumer acceptability and market value significantly influence it. These characteristics include variables such as grain size and shape, chalkiness, amylose concentration, and culinary attributes including texture and fragrance [ 9 ]. Optimal rice quality is crucial for satisfying consumer demands and improving market competitiveness, particularly in areas where rice is a fundamental food production. Consumers' growing selectivity over the sensory characteristics of the rice they consume has led to a rising demand for rice with certain quality features [ 10 ]. Hence, it is crucial to enhance both the productivity and the quality characteristics of rice in order to maintain its significance as a worldwide food crop. The largest intake was seen in various Asian nations, with Myanmar having the highest yearly consumption at 211 kg/person. The average amount of rice consumed worldwide in 1999 was 58 kg [ 5 ]. Furthermore, rice is the most important crop for the millions of small farmers who produce it throughout the region on millions of hectares, as well as for the countless landless workers who make a livelihood by working on these fields [ 11 ]. Among the six biggest producers of rice in the world, China, India, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Vietnam, and Thailand are responsible for producing more than three-quarters of the world's rice [ 12 ]. To meet the need for food brought on by population expansion and income-induced consumption, however, the world's yearly supply of rough rice will need to significantly expand during the next 30 years [ 13 ]. Rice is a basic diet for over 160 million people living in Bangladesh [ 14 ]. The rice sector is crucial, contributing to the majority of the nation s overall calorie supply, about half of the typical person's daily protein intake, and over 48% of rural employment [ 15 ]. Furthermore, rice production accounts for one-half of Bangladesh's agricultural GDP and one-sixth of the country's total revenue [ 15 ]. About 13 million agricultural families are engaged in rice cultivation across the country, with rice grown on approximately 10.5 million hectares of land over the past three decades [ 16 ]. During the year 1971, Bangladesh, with a population of around 70.88 million, generated a cumulative output of nearly 10.59 million tons of rice [ 16 ]. In light of the current population exceeding 160 million, rice cultivation continues to be a vital factor in meeting the nation's growing food needs. Expanding the cultivation of modern rice varieties over more than 66% of the nation's rice fields, which accounts for roughly 73% of the overall rice production, has significantly contributed to increasing output [ 17 ]. Over the next two decades, Bangladesh is projected to see a population surge of 30 million persons, resulting in an annual growth rate of 1.5 million people [ 18 ]. Yet, the overall rice growing area is expected to decrease from 10.71 million hectares to 10.28 million hectares. Hence, it is essential to increase the present rice production from 2.74 metric tons per hectare to 3.74 metric tons per hectare in order to fulfil the future food requirements [ 19 ]. The genetic improvement of rice is under pressure to increase its yield potential in irrigated and non-irrigated lands as it is the staple food of more than three billion people, due to the emerging challenges of an increasing population, shrinking arable lands, and escalating threats posed by climate change. To further this argument, more genetic variety and variability within the rice gene pool are required for use in breeding programs [ 20 ]. The genetic diversity of a population is a representation of the heritable variation that exists both within that population and between populations. The classification of the parental lines, the identification of heterotic groups, and the prediction of future hybrid performance all depend on knowledge of the genetic diversity and distances between breeding lines as well as the connection between genetic distances [ 21 ]. Several approaches can be used to determine genetic distance estimates for population grouping since it's important to comprehend the useful diversity that exists in the population panel [ 22 ]. Using multivariate analysis is one strategy. Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Cluster analysis, and Discriminate Analysis are examples of multivariate statistical methods [ 23 ]. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) may be used to detect patterns and eliminate duplication in data sets, even when crop species vary in terms of production and grain quality [ 24 ]. Considering the significance of PCA, a study on rice germplasm was conducted to analyze inter-componential features linked to yield and quality. In order to group the accessions, it is necessary to find and categorize maximal variability into total variability while taking into consideration various qualities and their interrelationships. The yield is a complex attribute that is influenced by several elements, including genetic and environmental variables. An essential genetic criterion that defines the usefulness of lines or genotypes for use as parents in breeding programs is the breeding value [ 25 ]. Breeders are currently concentrating their efforts on creating new, elite breeding lines that have the potential to displace the current variety in terms of greater biotic and abiotic tolerance, higher yield, and good stability [ 26 , 27 , 28 ]. In this study, the adaptability of 300 elite germplasms from the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) and Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI) was thoroughly examined throughout the four distinct regions of Bangladesh. With early maturity variety development, our study sought to identify the parents for yield and quality traits. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Source material and experimental site For characterization and assessment, 300 rice ( Oryza sativa L.) germplasms comprising advanced lines from International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) & released varieties from Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI), were employed (Supplementary Table 1). The experiments were carried out at four separate sites- Gazipur, Barishal, Cumilla and Rajshahi throughout the transplanted aman season (wet) 2018 (Table 1 ). Table 1 Experimental Site Information Full size table 2.2 Experimental design and cultural practices A partly replicated (P-rep) design with two replications was employed for the experiment. The plot had 5.4 m of length and 5 rows (5.4 m 2 ). 25-day-old seedlings were transplanted at a density of 2 3 plants per hill, spaced 20 cm apart. With split applications of N at 15, 30, and 50 days after transplanting (DAT), fertilizer doses of 120:19:60:20:3.6 kg/ha NPKSZn (260 97-120-110-11 kg/ha Urea-TSP-Gypsum-ZnSO4, respectively) were administered. At the time of the last stage of land preparation, a total of P K S Zn was applied. According to the need, weed control techniques and irrigation were used. 2.3 Data collection The study was conducted at the four different locations following p-rep design. Each trait, including plant height (PH), days to 50% flowering (DFF), days to maturity (DTM), effective tiller (ET), plot yield (YLD), grain length (GRL), and grain width (GRW), was measured according to the standard evaluation system (SES) for rice and amylose content (AC%), chalkiness (CHK), and zinc content (ZNC) was measured according to the standard protocols. When the genotypes were at their maturity stage, phenotypic data were acquired in order to precisely represent their performance. Following the methodology given by Juliano [ 29 ], the amylose content (AC%) of rice grain was obtained. Chalkiness % (CHK) was visually rated by us, and the SES scale served as the foundation for the determination of the rating. Jeffers [ 31 ] criteria guided the selection of principal components (PCs) with Eigenvalues larger than one. Using PC1 and PC2, the first two principal components, we created a biplot to visualize the genotype distribution. The degree of group differentiation was assessed using the Euclidean distance and the UPGMA (Unweighted Pair Group method with Arithmetic Mean) clustering algorithm. This analysis grouped the genotypes into clusters based on their genetic similarity. We used Best Linear Unbiased Prediction (BLUP) to estimate the genotypes' breeding values. Determined the selection index by allocating weights to the breeding values of various characteristics according to their comparative economic significance and heritability. All statistical analyses were conducted using R software (version 4.4.1), using many packages including asreml for BLUP, lme4 for mixed models, and standard functions for PCA and cluster analysis. 3 Results 3.1 Principal component analysis (PCA) The result presented the eigenvalues, the percentage of variance contribution, and the variable loadings for the four principal components (PCs) in Table 2 . Rice germplasm was used to perform principal component analysis on both quantitative and qualitative attributes. Principal Component 1 (PC1) had a higher proportion of variability, amounting to 34.857%, compared to the 28.99% reported by Kiani [ 33 ]. In contrast, Principal Components 2 and 3 (PC2 and PC3) contributed 14.686% and 12.776% respectively to the variety seen among the genotypes for the parameters under examination. According to the findings of the research carried out by Gour et al. [ 34 ], the component PC1 was responsible for 18.683 percent of the total variability. Furthermore, the variability contributions of PC2, PC3 and PC4 were discovered to be 14.686%, 12.776% and 9.859% respectively, as reported in Table 2 . The aforementioned results provide insights into the use of multivariate analysis in studying rice germplasm, with a particular focus on the importance of distinct principal components in understanding differences in traits and genetic diversity. The principal component analysis (PCA) successfully simplified the dataset, revealing that the top three PCs explained a substantial 62.319% of the overall variability. Consequently, the selection procedure for breeding is simplified since the bulk of the significant yield-contributing characteristics in the rice lines can be accounted for by a small number of critical parameters. The substantial eigenvalue of 3.486 in PC1 implies that factors like effective tiller number, amylose concentration, and zinc content significantly affect total variance. Therefore, breeding attempts to boost agricultural yield and nutritional value must prioritize these traits. From the scree plot, we were able to observe how much variance is accounted for by each principal component. This was made possible by the fact that the link between eigenvalues and principal component numbers was made extremely clear. The scree plot shows that the first few principal components, especially PC1, dominate the variability with the biggest variation. This supports the premise that discovering superior genotypes requires emphasis on leading PCs. The near-flat line after the first few PCs shows that additional components provide minimal information, simplifying the selection process to concentrate on the most important qualities. Accordingly, selecting lines from PCs 5, 7, 9, and 10 can be advantageous in rapidly improving yield-related characteristics. Additionally, selecting lines based on PC2 and PC8 can be beneficial for enhancing quality-related features [ 35 ]. It is worth noting that PC4 also influences yield-related characteristics [ 36 ], and plant height demonstrates undesirable behavior when PC8 is used for germplasm selection. The rotated component matrix shows which traits are most important in each principal component, like yield in PC7 and effective tiller in PC5. This detailed understanding enables breeders to target specific traits associated with yield improvements, plant height, or flowering time based on the desired outcome. For instance, if early maturity is a goal, focusing on traits in PC10, which include days to 50% flowering, would be strategic. The biplot analysis also finds genotypes that have good combinations of traits, like plant height and grain width. This is very important for choosing parents that have the right balance of yield potential and other important agronomic qualities. The first two principal components, PC1 and PC2, were plotted against each other inside this framework, which resulted in the generation of a biplot. When it comes to showing the connections that exist between variables and observations inside a two-dimensional domain, this graphical representation is an extremely helpful tool [ 32 ]. In the present biplot, a noticeable cluster, including 18 genotypes (specifically, genotypes 11, 31, 36, 48, 68, 78, 119, 126, 133, 195, 218, 220, 235, 241, 265, 266, 284, and 295) significantly manifested itself, occupying a prominent place in the top right quadrant. The observed genotypes had positive values for both principal component 1 (PC1) and principal component 2 (PC2), indicating that they displayed better attributes in terms of yield and quality-related factors when compared to the other rice lines [ 37 ]. It is worth mentioning that some characteristics, namely plant height (PH), days to 50% flowering (FLW), days to maturity (DTM), plot yield (YLD), and grain width (GRW), show a positive correlation with this particular set of genotypes (Fig. 3 ). The significant correlation between these genotypes highlights their substantial capacity to improve both the productivity and quality of rice. This study used UPGMA based clustering analysis, specifically applying the average linkage distance approach, to examine a dataset consisting of 300 advanced rice genotypes. The UPGMA cluster analysis reveals the emergence of discrete groups within the rice germplasm, each with particular characteristic profiles. As a result, the research successfully identified four unique groups within the dataset. These groups were given the following names: Cluster I, which included 77 genotypes; Cluster II, which included 125 genotypes; Cluster III, which included 13 genotypes; and Cluster IV, which included 82 genotypes. Cluster II, which has the highest mean values for several yield-related attributes, is an important group for breeding projects aimed at high-yielding cultivars. Cluster III, which has the lowest mean values, may reflect lines that are less suitable for direct yield enhancements but might be valuable in other situations, such as stress tolerance breeding [ 32 ]. Cluster means for numerous traits of elite rice germplasm accessions are shown in Table 5 . Cluster II had the most genotypes and average values of 99.2 cm in plant height, 90 days to 50% flowering, 13 effective tillers per plant, 3.7 t/ha in plot yield, 3.0 percent chalkiness, 6.4 mm in grain length, 2.2 mm in grain width, and most important trait for T. Aman season was 124 days to maturity, 24.9 percent amylose, 14.4 parts per million in zinc. Following Cluster IV where plant height (88 cm), plot yield (3.1 t/ha) and amylose content (22%) are below the acceptable range. Cluster I had the also low amylose content (22.6%) which was not acceptable. Finally, Cluster III had the fewest genotypes where poor grain quality shown i.e. low amylose content (20.8%) and higher percentage of chalkiness (4.3). This clustering trend aligns with previous investigations by Rahman et al. [ 38 ], Suh et al. [ 39 ], and Asante et al. [ 40 ]. Overall, cluster analysis provided an insight into the diversity of the collections as shown that Cluster II cover the all favourable yield contributing traits such as plant type, maturity, yield and grain quality traits amylose, chalkiness and zinc content. This means that genotypes from these groups may be used in future breeding program. The selection of the 92 genotypes was based on breeding value, and each one had to pass three local checks and provide a yield of more than four tons per hectare [ 41 , 42 ]. Subsequently, from these 92 genotypes, 86 genotypes were further selected based on the number of days needed to reach maturity falling between 120 and 135 [ 43 ]. As a result of this selection, the 86 genotypes were narrowed down to 67 genotypes that exhibited plant heights (cm) ranging from 97 to 110. Based on this criterion, 53 genotypes with amylose concentrations ranging from 20 to 27 percent were then chosen for further study [ 44 ]. Furthermore, 36 genotypes were selected based on the length of the grain (6.5 mm to 7.15 mm) and breadth of the grain (2.09 mm to 2.27 mm) [ 45 ]. During the conclusive phase of the selection process, six outstanding genotypes were identified, based on desirable qualities that required a zinc content over 13 ppm and a chalkiness level below 2 [ 46 ]. These six genotypes (86, 142, 143, 239, 282, and 295) have been chosen because they might be good candidates for a breeding effort with the objective of developing superior lines with improved control over high-quality attributes [ 47 ]. Paying attention to features like yield, early maturity, medium plant height, grain size, and zinc concentration suggests that the chosen genotypes will help create rice varieties that meet both agricultural and nutritional needs, especially in places where micronutrient deficiencies are common. 5 Conclusion A comprehensive investigation was conducted on a set of 300 exceptional rice germplasms that were supplied by the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) and Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI). This work made use of three basic methods for assessing breeding data: principal component analysis (PCA), cluster analysis and breeding value analysis (BV). The primary objective of the research was to identify genotypes that have superior characteristics with the purpose of using these genotypes in further breeding initiatives. In the UPGMA-based dendrogram, In the PCA scheme, Cluster II came out as the most promising. It was composed of 125 genotypes, each of which was outstanding in terms of the form of the plant, its growth, and the quality of the grain. It was decided to take into account properties such as amylose content, chalkiness, and zinc concentration because of their significant influence on yield. Biplot analysis, with a focus on the first two principal components (PC1 and PC2), demonstrated a positive link between certain genotypes identified in the upper right quadrant of the plot and significant agronomic parameters, such as plant height, flowering, and maturity dates, yield, and grain width. By analyzing the plot and concentrating on the first two main components, this was confirmed. The genotypes identified as 11, 31, 36, 48, 68, 78, 119, 126, 133, 195, 218, 220, 235, 241, 265, 266, 284, and 295 all had positive characteristics that show potential for increasing rice yields. The Breeding Value analysis detected another six genotypes (86, 142, 143, 239, 282 and 295) that can be considered for further breeding activities. Most importantly, genotype 295 (IRRI 154) outperformed as a male parent with distinctive features. The research highlights the efficacy of integrating morphological and breeding value analysis for the identification and selection of high-performing rice germplasm. The results also have practical consequences for the development of rice cultivars that enhance both productivity and nutritional value, especially in areas marked by micronutrient insufficiencies. Such untoward climatic shocks invariably hit almost all blocks of Puri District in Odisha. The variety-based climate-smart intervention proved to be a potential response in the flood-prone rice areas. This can be replicated and scaled up in other blocks within the district as part of contingency plans for rice-growing areas affected by floods in the state. Agriculture in Odisha, India added 20.6% to the Gross State Value in 2021-22 with the low-land coastal district of Puri as one of the major contributors, according to the Odisha Economic Survey. Topographically, 58% of the 0.189 million hectares of cultivated land in this geography are classified as shallow and deep lowlands, and the remaining is medium land. Rice, oilseeds, green and black grams, and vegetables (eggplant, potato, okra, cauliflower, and tomato) are the major crops grown during the wet and dry seasons. With a high irrigation coverage of 70% (from canals), the district has an impressive cropping intensity of 217%. Rice is the primary crop grown in the wet season and is planted on approximately 94,000 hectares mostly in the lowlands (88% of the total winter rice area). Despite the high irrigation coverage and the high proportion of fertile alluvial soils in more than half of the area favorable for rice cultivation, production, and productivity are seriously challenged by recurring floods (August to September), salinity (February to March), drought (mid-July), and occasional cyclonic storms (September to November). These natural calamities, primarily floods, of varying intensity adversely affect the standing crop leading to poor harvests. Such untoward climatic shocks invariably hit almost all blocks of Puri. The impact of the frequent flood crisis The southwest monsoon in the district normally sets in around the third week of June and withdraws in the last week of September. It brings an average of 1,061 mm of rainfall, which is 82% of the yearly precipitation. Based on this climatic norm and meteorological forecast, farmers normally transplant rice towards the end of July to mid-August. In 2022, heavy monsoon rains in early and mid-August, caused by a weather system over the Bay of Bengal, triggered several distributaries of the Mahanadi River to overflow and inundate vast tracts of newly transplanted rice areas in the district. Nimapara was among the areas where farmers suffered significant crop losses because of prolonged flooding. The Dhanua River that passes through Nimapada floods the villages of Kothakusang, Balange, and Bamanal for 15-25 days, depending upon soil topography and water drainage efficiency. The GIS Laboratory at the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) mapped the flooded tract in the district and estimated the affected area. Pre- (06 August) and post- (18 August) flood sentinel-1 SAR images corroborated the occurrence of high-intensity floods and detected a large impacted area. GIS-based estimation indicated that, in Nimapada alone, the flood affected 3,739 hectares of rice fields. Spatial flood inundation maps generated for Nimapara showed large rice areas under water. An estimated 12,563 ha rice area spread across blocks of Gop, Astaranga, Kaktapur, Nimapada, and Pipli were flooded for at least 10 days. Recommended contingency plan for the flood crisis In such a worst-case scenario, farmers need coping mechanisms to salvage crops and minimize seasonal crop losses. Plant flood-tolerant rice varieties. Farmers in the village planted high-yielding rice varieties including Swarna, Sarala, CR dhan-1018, among others that are prone to submergence. Thus, flood-induced crop damage could not be averted. Farmers in flood-prone lowland areas should plant long-duration (140-150 days) flood-tolerant rice varieties. Two established flood-tolerant rice varieties, CR 1009-Sub1, and Swarna-Sub1, can offset the impact of crop inundation and ensure a reasonable harvest. Although flood-tolerant rice varieties would have been a better choice, even these could fail if floodwaters remain stagnant for more than 15 days. Stagnant flood (SF) tolerance is needed but there are no known rice varieties that combine flood and SF tolerance that can withstand both flash and stagnant floods. Replant flood-damaged fields. After the flood water recedes, farmers can replant their fields with rice seedlings secured from other places to replace their damaged crops. However, not every farmer can afford and arrange for seedlings given the short period. Oftentimes, seedlings in nearby areas are hardly available. Even if they are, rice seedlings are often too old and no longer suitable for transplanting. Such challenges, along with logistical bottlenecks and increased production costs, deter farmers from replanting their flood-damaged lands. After suffering from crop losses in August, there is a small window for growing suitable early maturing rice varieties as a post-flood crop. If the post-flood field is managed agronomically, and farmers replant an early maturing variety (100-110 days) preferably using the wet direct-seeded rice (DSR) method, a reasonable yield is fairly assured. This is a better proposition than losing the entire crop and the land being fallow thereafter. Farmers usually hesitate to adopt the first two recommendations because of a lack of awareness about flood-tolerant varieties or the availability of seedlings for replanting. However, the third option could be operationally easier and more financially rewarding, But this coping mechanism have not been fully tested and promoted under the said conditions. A variety-based climate-smart intervention With its considerable research base in Odisha, IRRI curated a technical fix to address the impact of the climatic crisis. In association with Pragati Koraput, a non-government organization in Odisha, IRRI introduced variety-based intervention in four flood-affected villages in Nimapada in the first week of September. The intervention included 55 affected farmers covering 25 hectares of rice areas identified using data, GIS-enabled mapping, and field observations. Two early maturing varieties, CR dhan-101 (Ankit) and CR dhan-102 (Santabhima), were chosen based on their performance in earlier varietal evaluation programs conducted by the IRRI Seed System. These two varieties mature in 105-110 days, have an average yield of 4 tons/ha, and are moderately resistant to major diseases and pests. Because the maturity of these varieties fits within the short time window (September to December) for growing crops, these short-duration varieties could replace the yield of the late-maturing varieties lost to flooding. Field observations and learning To demonstrate the variety-based intervention, IRRI held several meetings and orientations to create awareness among the participating farmers. The IRRI Team encouraged farmers to sow the varieties using the wet DSR method in areas where drainage was feasible instead of traditional transplanting. The team also issued and shared recommended nutrient management advisories for the altered field ecology. The IRRI Team closely monitored the seed sowing, nutrient management practices, and the different phases of crop growth. Several post-flood rice plots that were fallowed after the flood damage served as the ideal control plot for assessing the intervention impact. During the interaction between IRRI scientists and participating farmers, it was determined that only a few farmers could manage to acquire some seedlings from other villages to replant and harvest a moderate crop. Those who did not have that option were forced to keep their land fallow. As a result, large swathes of land were uncultivated following the flood. How the variety-based intervention could help farmers The farmers under the intervention, however, have a reason to smile. The early maturing varieties flourished and yielded at least 3.5 tons/ha. The good productivity of the recommended varieties could help farmers make up for the losses due to floods. Even if farmers suffer from crop damage due to flooding in September, they could still grow the recommended rice varieties and have a respectable harvest. Thus, the varieties could act as stand-by crops that farmers can sow, rather than fallowing, if the first late-maturing variety succumbs to floods My land was about to lie vacant this season after the flood, said Mr.Bijay Kumar Singh a farmer who was part of the program. But with Ankit, I harvested a decent yield comparable to the damaged and lost yield of Swarna and CR-1009. The recommended varieties matured in time (mid-December) enabling the field to be free for the farmers to sow the next crops mostly summer rice, green gram, and vegetables. Other local farmers stated that these varieties could potentially alter the lives of hundreds of small and marginal farmers with limited resources. Wet-DSR was a suggested option but farmers preferred to opt to raise nurseries and transplant early, reducing the risk of losing the crop due to further flooding. Rice as a contingency crop Because of the low-lying land in the region, early-maturing varieties are not best-fit options under normal scenarios; hence farmers were not aware of these varieties. Raising awareness of these varieties through this intervention empowers farmers to formulate a crop contingency plan for the next season. Almost all the participating farmers will keep some seeds of these varieties as part of a contingency plan next year, said Mr. Ramesh Chandra Mangaraj, another program participant who immensely benefited from the intervention. The variety-based intervention proved to be a pertinent and potential response in flood-prone rice areas. This can be replicated and scaled up in other blocks within the district and beyond. IRRI will share such evidence-backed experience with district and state agriculture departments as it can be suitably included in a contingency plan for flood-affected rice growing areas in the state. With the learning and insights from these field-based interventions, IRRI will facilitate need-based targeting of the area in 2024 and emphasize building farmers capacity to better manage flood-related farm losses. IRRI will also support agencies and machinery to boost the popularity and significance of specific varieties through other innovative extension methods. Engagement with important seed system stakeholders can further disseminate these varieties and amplify seed production. IRRI will further diffuse this response with the grassroots-level organizations in the region that worked with IRRI, directly or indirectly. To take on complex problems, solutions need to be fostered and advanced collectively by all key stakeholders to best serve farmers interests.
