August 19, 2024 | By IWMI By Louise Sarant IWMI presented recent scientific advances and innovative solutions developed with local partners to improve water productivity, availability, and overall resilience of Morocco s three main river basins: Souss-Massa, Bouregreg, and Oum Er-Rbia. In the central-western part of Morocco, the Souss-Massa basin grapples with dwindling freshwater resources resulting from prolonged drought, extreme heat, and increasing water demand for irrigation. To better track water availability and usage, IWMI, along with the Watershed Agency of Souss-Massa and the Regional Office of Agricultural Development, has developed a Dynamic Water Accounting Dashboard under F2R-CWANA, CGIAR s leading initiative on resilient food systems. The dashboard uses crucial data from local partners related to water, climate, and agriculture, helping decision-makers manage the limited freshwater resources in the basin fairly and effectively. Reduced rainfall and land degradation are negatively impacting the Bouregreg basin, which provides drinking water for 6 million people in Rabat, parts of Casablanca, and surrounding areas. To assess Bouregreg s water and agricultural systems susceptibility to climate-related hazards, IWMI, under F2R-CWANA, developed a Fragility Analysis Framework in partnership with the Watershed Agency of Bouregreg and Chaouia. This framework assesses the severity of droughts, erosion and floods under current and future scenarios. Among Morocco s 12 major river basins, the Oum Er-Rbia basin is experiencing the most significant water deficit. This basin is located in central-western Morocco, an area known for its olives, milk, pomegranates and sweet paprika. IWMI scientists presented their Multiscale Polycentric Governance model for Oum Er-Rbia, developed under ClimBER CGIAR s main initiative focused on climate resilience. This governance approach, in the early stages of development in Morocco, seeks to enhance stakeholder collaboration and institutional cohesion to boost water productivity and youth employment in Morocco s olive and milk value chains. This work involves collaboration with several organizations, including the Ministry of Agriculture s Directorate of Strategy and Statistics, the Regional Office of Agricultural Development of Tadla, and the Watershed Agency of Oum Er-Rbia. Morocco s growing interest in reusing treated wastewater for agriculture IWMI signed an MoU with the Directorate of Irrigation and Agricultural Land Development (DIAEA) of the Ministry of Agriculture to boost wastewater reuse in agriculture and enhance productivity using digital solutions. IWMI signed a second MoU with the National Association of Land Improvements, Irrigation, Drainage, and Environment (ANAFIDE), to promote science-policy dialogue and capacity-building for wastewater treatment and reuse in Morocco. As the only freshwater source that grows with GDP, Morocco is increasingly interested in reusing treated wastewater for agricultural purposes. While the kingdom has been successful in irrigating golf courses and green spaces with treated wastewater, pilots experimenting with agriculture applications have faced challenges. To address this, IWMI, in collaboration with ANAFIDE, the Directorate of Irrigation and Agricultural Land Development and the Directorate of Water Research and Planning is developing a cost-benefit analysis framework for agricultural reuse of treated wastewater. This work is supported by the CGIAR Initiative on Fragility to Resilience in Central and West Asia and North Africa. Its goal is to assess the economic and social benefits of wastewater reuse, with the Imzouren wastewater treatment plant in Al Hoceima serving as the pilot site for this analysis. The way forward for IWMI in Morocco Moving forward, IWMI aims to enhance collaboration with its Moroccan partners and leverage the collective knowledge and expertise of all stakeholders to ensure Morocco s water and food security in an increasingly volatile climate. As Youssef Brouziyne, IWMI Representative in the MENA region, stated, In our collaborative efforts, we see not only challenges but also immense opportunities for innovation and partnership that can propel Morocco toward an increasingly resilient and sustainable future. The Morocco Resilience Days forum was held from June 25-28, 2024, in Rabat, bringing together 280 delegates from 44 institutions. The forum was a collaboration between IWMI and Morocco s Ministry of Agriculture, Maritime Fisheries, Rural Development, and Water and Forest with the support of the Ministry of Equipment and Water. Title: IWMI signs MoU with the League of Arab States: The agreement will facilitate further cooperation in the water security agenda of the Arab region [blog]
Description: This blog discusses how IWMI and the League of Arab States (LAS) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in Cairo in August 2024 to strengthen collaboration on regional water security. Signed by Youssef Brouziyne, IWMI’s Regional Representative for MENA, and Ambassador Shahira Wahbi, Director of LAS’s Department of Housing, Water Resources, and Disaster Reduction, the MoU aims to align research and development strategies and enhance communication on programming and activities. IWMI will support the implementation of SAMWC recommendations, while SAMWC will utilize IWMI’s research to address critical water challenges. Priority areas include groundwater sustainability, wastewater reuse, policy coherence, and digital irrigation tools. Brouziyne emphasized the importance of this milestone, highlighting the partnership’s potential to confront water and climate challenges in the MENA region. Through this agreement, IWMI and LAS aim to enhance regional coordination and advance sustainable water management initiatives.

August 29, 2024 | By IWMI By Jialan Deal The International Water Management Institute (IWMI) and the League of Arab States (LAS) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) last week in Cairo, Egypt. The agreement was signed on behalf of IWMI by Youssef Brouziyne, Regional Representative in the Middle East and North Africa, and Ambassador Shahira Wahbi, Director of the Department of Housing, Water Resources, and Disaster Reduction of the LAS. Under this agreement, the Secretariat of the Arab Ministerial Water Council (SAMWC) of the LAS and IWMI will exchange their research and development agenda and strategies for better collaboration on regional water security. The two parties also committed to more active communication on programming and activities. Moving forward, IWMI will review the implementation of SAMWC recommendations with its partners in member states, and SAMWC pledged to utilize the results of development research and studies carried out by IWMI. Brouziyne said, I am pleased to celebrate this important milestone for IWMI in the region. Strategic cooperation with the League of Arab States means better alignment between IWMI s research agenda and the joint efforts of Arab states for water security. I look forward to this agreement leading to a closer partnership as we confront the water and climate challenges in the MENA region together. With this MoU, IWMI and the LAS will continue to address joint topics of high priority such as groundwater sustainability, wastewater treatment and reuse, coherence of water and agricultural policies and the use of digital tools in irrigation management. Through partnerships with the LAS and other relevant stakeholders, IWMI seeks to enhance regional coordination on water security goals. The two parties also committed to more active communication on programming and activities. Moving forward, IWMI will review the implementation of SAMWC recommendations with its partners in member states, and SAMWC pledged to utilize the results of development research and studies carried out by IWMI. Brouziyne said, I am pleased to celebrate this important milestone for IWMI in the region. Strategic cooperation with the League of Arab States means better alignment between IWMI s research agenda and the joint efforts of Arab states for water security. I look forward to this agreement leading to a closer partnership as we confront the water and climate challenges in the MENA region together. With this MoU, IWMI and the LAS will continue to address joint topics of high priority such as groundwater sustainability, wastewater treatment and reuse, coherence of water and agricultural policies and the use of digital tools in irrigation management. Through partnerships with the LAS and other relevant stakeholders, IWMI seeks to enhance regional coordination on water security goals. Descripción.
La tercera versión del Congreso Internacional Theobroma Para la Paz se desarrolló entre los días 16 y 20 de septiembre de 2024 en el edificio Yapurá de la sede centro de la Universidad de la Amazonia. La realización del evento fue organizada por la Universidad de la Amazonia y el apoyo de la Alianza Bioversity & CIAT y contó con el patrocinio de 18 instituciones de orden nacional e internacional. Esta versión del congreso contó con una agenda diversificada que incorporó el Segundo Concurso Nacional de Chocolate Artesanal de Mesa “Aromas y Sabores de Paz”, la Primera Feria Comercial Theobroma Emprende Innovando Para la Paz y 14 cursos postcongreso. En cuanto a participación, el congreso contó con una asistencia superior a las 700 personas entre asistentes a las sesiones de ponencias y asistentes a cursos postcongreso, contando con participación de productores, transformadores, asistentes técnicos, investigadores, gestores sociales, estudiantes y demás personal relacionado a la cadena de valor del cultivo de cacao.
Bajo el lema “Uniendo saberes para una cacaocultura incluyente” y con una participación total de 38 ponentes, entre los que se encuentran nueve internacionales y veintinueve ponentes nacionales (Anexo 1), esta versión del congreso incorporó las líneas temáticas de calidad de suelos; productividad y manejo agronómico; calidad de grano, agroindustria y comercialización y cacaocultura climáticamente inteligente, la cuales se desarrollaron a través de diferentes ponencias y cursos postcongreso. Además de esto incorporó charlas magistrales que permitieron abortar temáticas sobre cadmio, sistemas agroforestales con cacao, análisis sensorial y deforestación, lo que permitió una un intercambio de saberes entre la comunidad académica, las asociaciones de productores, emprendimientos de transformación y comercialización y la población general, aportando así a la formación de capital humano y el desarrollo del sector cacaotero.

Diferente a los agrobosques, existen cultivos diversificados o policultivos, los cuales combinan diversas especies de uso agrícola con una orientación mas comercial. En este sentido, asociar especies que permitan la existencia de multiestratos en las plantaciones de cacao es de vital importancia dado el papel crucial que juega la sombra para este cultivo, la cual aporta beneficios ecológicos, productivos y de reducción de las emisiones de CO2.
No obstante, las plantaciones de cacao requieren de procesos de renovación. En este sentido existen diversas posibilidades como la renovación total o escalonada. El enfoque de renovación incluye herramientas económicas como el valor presente neto (NPV) para determinar el momento adecuado para reemplazar un cacaotal. Existen diversos modelos que permiten analizar las interacciones entre los componentes de un agroecosistema de manera que se pueda estimar el tiempo apropiado para su renovación.
Finalmente, la presentación resalta la necesidad de diseños personalizados para cada finca, utilizando modelos dinámicos y la participación activa de productores en el diseño y evaluación de prototipos. Las decisiones sobre renovación dependen de factores como la rentabilidad, la biodiversidad y las expectativas de mercado, enfatizando un manejo integral y adaptado para garantizar la sostenibilidad económica y ambiental del cultivo.

Esta ponencia permite abordar diferentes retos a los cuales se enfrenta la industria del cultivo de cacao en Latinoamérica, siendo uno de los de mayor relevancia el desconocimiento del calidad del cacao, la cual es comprometida por la necesidad de producir en gran cantidad. Esta degradación en la calidad del cacao producido tiene implicaciones económicas para los agricultores, y compromete con ello el acceso a mercados internacionales y especializados en cacao de calidad. En este sentido, se hace énfasis en la necesidad de fortalecer procesos que permitan una mejor trazabilidad a lo largo de la cadena productiva, de manera que se pueda minimizar los factores que comprometen la calidad del producto.
De acuerdo con la ponente, existen diferentes estrategias que permiten hacer frente a la degradación de la calidad en la producción de cacao, siendo el fomento del análisis sensorial una de ellas. A través de estos análisis, tanto productores como consumidores pueden tener un mejor conocimiento de las características del cacao fino y su potencial en la elaboración de chocolate de alta calidad, razón por la cual es necesario ahondar esfuerzos en la formación de capital humano en términos de catación y técnicas de análisis sensorial elevar los estándares de calidad en la producción de cacao. Ponencia: Estrategias de investigación para la mitigación de absorción de cadmio (Cd) en granos de cacao.
Ponente: Mirjam Pulleman
Institución: Alianza Bioversity International – CIAT
La ponencia aborda como problema central la existencia de cadmio (Cd) en los suelos de cultivos de cacao en Latinoamérica, el cual está presente de forma natural y es agravado por las acciones antropogénicas como el uso de fertilizantes sintéticos. La absorción de este metal por parte de las plantas y acumulación en sus partes útiles para consumo humano, como lo son los granos de cacao representa un alto riesgo para la salud humana, dada su toxicidad y carencia de funciones biológicas dentro de un organismo vivo. Esto a su vez afecta de manera significativa su comercialización, trayendo consigo impactos negativos en las regiones productoras y en consecuencia, a sus cultivadores.
En este contexto, diferentes acciones interdisciplinarias se han adelantado como estrategia para hacer frente a esta problemática, dando como resultado una serie de actividades que mitigan este fenómeno. Dentro de estas actividades se encuentran el uso de variedades genéticas con menor capacidad de absorción de este metal, enmiendas edáficas y prácticas de postcosecha. Sin embargo, y pese a los avances hechos en aras de disminuir la presencia de Cd en el cacao, en la actualidad se estima que un 50% del grano producido posee niveles superiores a los estándares permitidos, generando así afectaciones económicas a productores. Como solución rápida a este problema, se emplean estrategias como la mezcla de grano de diferentes orígenes, lo cual resulta en una disminución de la concentración del metal, sin embargo, dar solución a esta problemática requiere de esfuerzos a largo plazo, los cuales combinen estrategias como el mejoramiento genético, practicas diferenciadas para los territorios, y enfoques de co-desarrollo a través de los cuales se vincule el personal de toda la cadena productiva junto con personal científico, de manera que se puedan ahondar esfuerzos que permitan la co-creación de estrategias para garantizar la sostenibilidad y viabilidad de las prácticas de mitigación.

Esta ponencia aborda el cacao como una alternativa para la restauración socioambiental en zonas afectadas por el conflicto en Colombia. En este sentido, se menciona la relevancia que posee el sector cacaotero en Colombia como herramienta y motor de cambio con un alto potencial para la producción sostenible, la restauración de áreas degradadas y el desarrollo social. De acuerdo con la ponencia, el cacao genera impactos positivos en aspectos ecológicos y sociales, sin embargo, también presenta retos como la deforestación, la presencia de cadmio y la necesidad de mejorar las capacidades de los agricultores que hacen necesarias acciones para generar sostenibilidad en la producción. En la ponencia se expone que, aunque algunos productores generan implementaciones de cultivos en modelos alternativos como los SAF, estas acciones no contrarrestan problemas como la deforestación, generando así que la actual producción sostenible de cacao no es un negocio rentable.
Para afrontar estos desafíos, se proponen estrategias como la caracterización de las cadenas de valor, el diagnóstico de limitantes para la adopción de prácticas sostenibles y la implementación de un plan de acción. Se busca atraer inversión privada y aumentar la inversión pública en programas de desarrollo rural y sostenibilidad, así como promover la participación en mercados de carbono y mecanismos de pago por servicios ambientales. Finalmente, se resalta la importancia de la innovación financiera y el empoderamiento local, así como la necesidad de fortalecer capacidades en los agricultores cacaoteros afectados por el conflicto armado. La presentación concluye con un llamado a escalar modelos exitosos y a fomentar la investigación y el desarrollo en el sector cacaotero.

De acuerdo con la ponencia, la contaminación por Cd es uno de los principales problemas que enfrenta actualmente la cacaocultura, dados los efectos que este metal puede generar en la salud humana. Este problema es de vital importancia ya que limita el acceso a los mercados, dificultando los procesos de comercialización de grano, y es agravado por el desconocimiento de las regiones con presencia de Cd y con ello, la inadecuada gestión de estrategias para mitigar el problema. En este contexto, esta ponencia expone los resultados de un trabajo de investigación que tuvo como objetivo crear un mapa que ilustre la concentración de Cd en granos de cacao en diferentes regiones del territorio colombiano y a su vez, las estrategias de biorremediación implementadas.
El proceso de elaboración de este mapa se llevó a cabo a cabo a través de la recolección de muestras de suelo y grano de cacao en las diferentes zonas productoras. Posteriormente, estas muestras fueron analizadas en laboratorio para determinar su concentración de Cd, con lo cual se creó el mapa de distribución. Este resultado es de gran importancia dado que además de identificar las zonas afectadas por el Cd, facilita la adecuada gestión de procesos enfocados a mitigar el problema a través de estrategias como la biorremediación la cual tiene como propósito el uso de microorganismos capaces de reducir la concentración de este metal en el suelo. Sin embargo, además de conocer las zonas de afectación, la ponencia hace énfasis en la necesidad de capacitar a los productores en prácticas de manejo sostenible y los efectos nocivos generados por la contaminación con Cd, dado que una adecuada gestión de los cultivos en aspectos como la fertilización puede ser fundamental para disminuir las concentraciones de este metal en el grano.
Como último aspecto, la ponencia enfatiza en la necesidad de adelantar trabajos articulados destinados a la promoción de investigaciones para el desarrollo de tecnologías para la mitigación del Cd, así como en la concientización de los consumidores sobre la calidad del cacao y el riesgo de los metales pesados en los alimentos.

Descripción.
La tercera versión del Congreso Internacional Theobroma Para la Paz se desarrolló entre los días 16 y 20 de septiembre de 2024 en el edificio Yapurá de la sede centro de la Universidad de la Amazonia. La realización del evento fue organizada por la Universidad de la Amazonia y el apoyo de la Alianza Bioversity & CIAT y contó con el patrocinio de 18 instituciones de orden nacional e internacional. Esta versión del congreso contó con una agenda diversificada que incorporó el Segundo Concurso Nacional de Chocolate Artesanal de Mesa “Aromas y Sabores de Paz”, la Primera Feria Comercial Theobroma Emprende Innovando Para la Paz y 14 cursos postcongreso. En cuanto a participación, el congreso contó con una asistencia superior a las 700 personas entre asistentes a las sesiones de ponencias y asistentes a cursos postcongreso, contando con participación de productores, transformadores, asistentes técnicos, investigadores, gestores sociales, estudiantes y demás personal relacionado a la cadena de valor del cultivo de cacao.
Bajo el lema “Uniendo saberes para una cacaocultura incluyente” y con una participación total de 38 ponentes, entre los que se encuentran nueve internacionales y veintinueve ponentes nacionales (Anexo 1), esta versión del congreso incorporó las líneas temáticas de calidad de suelos; productividad y manejo agronómico; calidad de grano, agroindustria y comercialización y cacaocultura climáticamente inteligente, la cuales se desarrollaron a través de diferentes ponencias y cursos postcongreso. Además de esto incorporó charlas magistrales que permitieron abortar temáticas sobre cadmio, sistemas agroforestales con cacao, análisis sensorial y deforestación, lo que permitió una un intercambio de saberes entre la comunidad académica, las asociaciones de productores, emprendimientos de transformación y comercialización y la población general, aportando así a la formación de capital humano y el desarrollo del sector cacaotero.

Ponencia: Estrategias de investigación para la mitigación de absorción de cadmio (Cd) en granos de cacao.
Ponente: Mirjam Pulleman
Institución: Alianza Bioversity International – CIAT
La ponencia aborda como problema central la existencia de cadmio (Cd) en los suelos de cultivos de cacao en Latinoamérica, el cual está presente de forma natural y es agravado por las acciones antropogénicas como el uso de fertilizantes sintéticos. La absorción de este metal por parte de las plantas y acumulación en sus partes útiles para consumo humano, como lo son los granos de cacao representa un alto riesgo para la salud humana, dada su toxicidad y carencia de funciones biológicas dentro de un organismo vivo. Esto a su vez afecta de manera significativa su comercialización, trayendo consigo impactos negativos en las regiones productoras y en consecuencia, a sus cultivadores.
En este contexto, diferentes acciones interdisciplinarias se han adelantado como estrategia para hacer frente a esta problemática, dando como resultado una serie de actividades que mitigan este fenómeno. Dentro de estas actividades se encuentran el uso de variedades genéticas con menor capacidad de absorción de este metal, enmiendas edáficas y prácticas de postcosecha. Sin embargo, y pese a los avances hechos en aras de disminuir la presencia de Cd en el cacao, en la actualidad se estima que un 50% del grano producido posee niveles superiores a los estándares permitidos, generando así afectaciones económicas a productores. Como solución rápida a este problema, se emplean estrategias como la mezcla de grano de diferentes orígenes, lo cual resulta en una disminución de la concentración del metal, sin embargo, dar solución a esta problemática requiere de esfuerzos a largo plazo, los cuales combinen estrategias como el mejoramiento genético, practicas diferenciadas para los territorios, y enfoques de co-desarrollo a través de los cuales se vincule el personal de toda la cadena productiva junto con personal científico, de manera que se puedan ahondar esfuerzos que permitan la co-creación de estrategias para garantizar la sostenibilidad y viabilidad de las prácticas de mitigación.

De acuerdo con la ponencia, la contaminación por Cd es uno de los principales problemas que enfrenta actualmente la cacaocultura, dados los efectos que este metal puede generar en la salud humana. Este problema es de vital importancia ya que limita el acceso a los mercados, dificultando los procesos de comercialización de grano, y es agravado por el desconocimiento de las regiones con presencia de Cd y con ello, la inadecuada gestión de estrategias para mitigar el problema. En este contexto, esta ponencia expone los resultados de un trabajo de investigación que tuvo como objetivo crear un mapa que ilustre la concentración de Cd en granos de cacao en diferentes regiones del territorio colombiano y a su vez, las estrategias de biorremediación implementadas.
El proceso de elaboración de este mapa se llevó a cabo a cabo a través de la recolección de muestras de suelo y grano de cacao en las diferentes zonas productoras. Posteriormente, estas muestras fueron analizadas en laboratorio para determinar su concentración de Cd, con lo cual se creó el mapa de distribución. Este resultado es de gran importancia dado que además de identificar las zonas afectadas por el Cd, facilita la adecuada gestión de procesos enfocados a mitigar el problema a través de estrategias como la biorremediación la cual tiene como propósito el uso de microorganismos capaces de reducir la concentración de este metal en el suelo. Sin embargo, además de conocer las zonas de afectación, la ponencia hace énfasis en la necesidad de capacitar a los productores en prácticas de manejo sostenible y los efectos nocivos generados por la contaminación con Cd, dado que una adecuada gestión de los cultivos en aspectos como la fertilización puede ser fundamental para disminuir las concentraciones de este metal en el grano.
Como último aspecto, la ponencia enfatiza en la necesidad de adelantar trabajos articulados destinados a la promoción de investigaciones para el desarrollo de tecnologías para la mitigación del Cd, así como en la concientización de los consumidores sobre la calidad del cacao y el riesgo de los metales pesados en los alimentos.

The support to SMEs has contributed to strengthening the appeal of agricultural innovation s to impact investors and unlocking funding by fast-tracking investment readiness, and equipping agribusinesses with the skills to design market-driven products that can successfully commercialize their innovations. The bootcamp emphasized the growing importance of impact measurement in the agribusiness sector, where demonstrating social, environmental, and economic impacts can attract and engage investors more effectively. Together, we can foster a successful ecosystem that benefits all stakeholders, from smallholder farmers to investors. Title: The CGIAR Food Systems Accelerator (CFSA) hosted Pitch Day in South Africa, bringing together agribusiness founders, investors, and researchers to foster partnerships and drive sustainable agricultural innovation in Africa
Description: The CGIAR Food Systems Accelerator (CFSA) Pitch Day, held on November 14–15, 2024, in Cape Town, South Africa, was a transformative event aimed at bridging the gaps between agribusiness founders, agribusiness innovations and investment. Under the theme Seeding the Future, the event provided a dynamic platform for entrepreneurs, investors, researchers, and ecosystem enablers to collaborate and forge impactful partnerships. At its core, the event underscored the critical role of investor relationships in scaling agribusinesses. These connections, founded on shared values and long-term objectives, are essential for driving sustainable agricultural development across the region.

By: Caroline Musau and Nathanial Peterson Pitch Day: Catalyzing Stronger Investor Relationships in Agriculture The CGIAR Food Systems Accelerator (CFSA) Pitch Day, held on November 14 15, 2024, in Cape Town, South Africa, was a transformative event aimed at bridging the gaps between agribusiness founders, agribusiness innovations and investment. Under the theme Seeding the Future, the event provided a dynamic platform for entrepreneurs, investors, researchers, and ecosystem enablers to collaborate and forge impactful partnerships. At its core, the event underscored the critical role of investor relationships in scaling agribusinesses. These connections, founded on shared values and long-term objectives, are essential for driving sustainable agricultural development across the region. Building Connections: Entrepreneurs, Researchers, and Investors CFSA Pitch Day created a unique nexus for collaboration, enabling stakeholders to address systemic agricultural challenges together. Agribusinesses benefited from meaningful interactions with both investors and researchers, gaining insights into how science-backed solutions can enhance their business models and mitigate risks for investors. The event s structure fostered a balance of formal and informal interactions. The main Pitch Day on November 14, 2024, featured 14 agribusinesses from Kenya, Zambia, Zimbabwe, and Malawi delivering compelling six-minute presentations, followed by dynamic Q&A sessions. These engagements allowed investors to gain deeper insights into the businesses profitability, climate-smart agriculture practices, and social impact strategies. To further strengthen connections, curated matchmaking sessions during breaks connected entrepreneurs with investors, CGIAR scientists, and support organizations. Following the pitch event, a cocktail forum provided a relaxed setting for participants to exchange ideas informally, with many choosing to extend their conversations late into the evening, thereby strengthening connections and expanding their perceptions of agribusiness success. The following day s picturesque wine farm tours offered a serene backdrop for meaningful conversations. Divided into smaller groups, the 60 participants explored commercial wine farming practices and deepened their relationships through extended discussions. This combination of structured presentations and casual networking created an ideal environment for participants to build trust, explore synergies, and discuss future opportunities in an open and collaborative setting. As one participant noted: I learned a lot from the Pitch Day and social interactions. I like the initiative and hope it continues I would love to stay engaged and help in whichever way I can. (Anthony Kimani, Venture Builder, Delta40 Ventures) Event Highlights Pitch Presentations The judges, drawn from the investment and banking sectors, were introduced to the participants and guided through the judging criteria. These criteria emphasized the ability to clearly articulate a business model, showcase value propositions and impact, and demonstrate commercial viability alongside strong team composition. Each agribusiness was given six minutes to pitch, followed by a Q&A session. A total of 14 agribusinesses from Kenya, Zambia, Zimbabwe, and Malawi spanning various value chains and at different growth stages, including ag-tech, processing, and aggregator firms took the stage. The entrepreneurs delivered compelling presentations, highlighting how their models integrate profitability with climate-smart agriculture and social impact. Standout Innovations Winner: Sesame for Life Location: Zimbabwe Sesame for Life operates an out-grower scheme that supplies smallholder farmers with essential inputs and training, enabling them to cultivate high-quality sesame for export. Farmers enter contracts to sell their harvest back to the company, creating a sustainable supply chain. Zimbabwean sesame, known for its high oil content, is ideal for oil production and increasingly sought after for tahini manufacturing. Runner-Up: Nyota Location: Kenya Nyota, a social enterprise in Kenya, collaborates with smallholder farmers to produce nutritious food. Farmers supply fresh vegetables for Nyota s frozen and canned specialty sauces, targeting middle-income urban consumers. By providing a reliable market, Nyota increases farmer incomes, reduces post-harvest losses, and enhances community nutrition. The enterprise also ensures a year-round supply of affordable, locally sourced frozen vegetables at stable prices, improving food availability. Second Runner-Up: Ndkay Zambia Location: Zambia Ndkay Zambia Limited is a renewable energy company that empowers smallholder farmers and marketeers with solar-powered solutions. These include solar cold rooms for produce storage to extend shelf life and reduce post-harvest losses, as well as solar irrigation systems that boost productivity, water efficiency, and climate resilience. Through accessible payment plans, Ndkay supports sustainable agricultural growth by enabling efficient water usage, maintaining produce quality, and providing reliable access to off-grid electricity. Addressing Key Challenges in Agribusiness Financing Agribusinesses in East and Southern Africa face significant barriers to accessing capital and building relationships with capital providers. These challenges are particularly pronounced in underserved regions, where: Limited Access to Investors: Many agribusinesses struggle to connect with investors aligned with their growth and impact goals. Mismatch Between Capital and Needs: Entrepreneurs often face difficulties navigating available financing options, such as equity or debt, which may not align with their business readiness or growth stage. Fragmented Ecosystems: A lack of cohesive networks and platforms inhibits the ability of agribusinesses to showcase their innovations effectively. CFSA Pitch Day addressed these gaps by: Facilitating meaningful conversations between agribusinesses and investors to align on shared objectives. Thank you for the invitation! It was truly insightful, and I appreciated the opportunity to network with new faces in our shared industry. (Martha Wairimu, Investment Manager, Iungo Capital) Providing a platform for researchers and investors to identify synergies in de-risking agribusinesses through science-backed solutions. Highlighting scalable and sustainable business models tailored to the realities of agribusinesses in east and southern Africa. Creating an immersive, three-day environment that encouraged trust-building, deep understanding, and ongoing collaboration. As one attendee observed: There is a place for science, agribusiness, and investors to collaborate and come up with solutions that answer to the needs of the world. (Jonathan Mwewa, Program Manager, Ndkay Zambia Limited) Insights from Event Speakers 1. Welcome Note by Nick Meehan, New Zealand Deputy High Commissioner, Pretoria The event began with an address by Nick Meehan who underscored the commitment of the Government of New Zealand to supporting programs focused on climate adaptation and mitigation in East and Southern Africa. Highlighting Ukama Ustawi as an example, he emphasized the critical role agriculture plays in combating climate change, both in New Zealand and Africa, where it contributes significantly to GDP. Nick called for a collaborative approach to tackle challenges faced by smallholder farmers in Africa and stressed the importance of funding Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs). He elaborated on their pivotal role in driving innovation, job creation, and sustainable economic growth. Quoting his address, he said: Events like the CFSA Pitch Day help support the ideas and collaborations required to reshape agri-food systems into sustainable and resilient ones. They create supportive environments for developing solutions and provide frameworks for entrepreneurs to embrace innovative approaches that can enhance productivity. He concluded his remarks by encouraging agribusinesses to leverage such platforms to foster innovation, collaboration, and progress. 2. Climate Finance in Sub-Saharan Africa Claris Parenti, Agrifood Systems Analyst at Climate Policy Initiative (CPI), shared insights on the Climate Finance Landscape in Sub-Saharan Africa, highlighting the need for increased funding in Agriculture, Forestry, and Other Land Use (AFOLU) sectors, which account for over 50% of emissions but receive only 20% of climate finance. She emphasized supporting early-stage businesses with climate solutions, aligning them with investor expectations, and providing tools to communicate their environmental and social impact effectively. 3. Impact Measurement for Agribusinesses Valentina Giombini, Research Officer at the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT, discussed how agribusinesses drive impact by improving rural livelihoods, enhancing biodiversity, and mitigating climate change through sustainable practices. She introduced practical frameworks for measuring impact, including causal chains and reliable indicators, and shared tailored pathways to help SMEs effectively engage investors and showcase their contributions. Key Outcomes Pipeline of Investable Agribusinesses: 14 businesses were identified for follow-up discussions, with 100% of investors expressing interest in proceeding with funding. A deal book featuring all 14 agribusinesses and 10 additional agribusinesses from Cohort 1 was shared with investors. Enhanced Capacity of Entrepreneurs: Participants reported a 100% improvement in their ability to articulate value propositions. Strengthened Investor Relationships: The extended three-day engagement enabled agribusinesses and investors to build trust, better understand each other s goals, and forge ongoing conversations. It was great to meet the companies you showcased and connect with other investors and experts in the agri-space. (Vera Wachira, Impact Investor, Hooge Raedt Social Ventures) Ecosystem Collaboration: Partnerships were initiated between agribusinesses, ESOs, and technical advisors. This was a program worth attending. Lots of takeaways and broader networks for sure (Victoria Mwafulirwa, Founder, Homes Industries) Thank you for initiating the VR project for us. My guys are super elated already. Would not have been possible without your support. (Florence Mogere, Founder, Nyota Limited) Looking Ahead: Scaling Partnerships for Impact CFSA Pitch Day served as a critical milestone in bridging agribusinesses with investors dedicated to fostering transformative and sustainable solutions. Building on the momentum from the event, the focus now turns to: Scaling climate-smart innovations to reach and benefit more farmers and communities. Diagnose and strengthen ecosystems that support sustainable and inclusive agriculture based on what we ve learned our companies need to scale successfully. Promoting collaboration on specific risks, like market access, water management, financing of new technologies and logistics coordination, to address systemic challenges in the food system. The impact of CFSA Pitch Day lies in its ability to break down barriers, create meaningful connections, and lay the groundwork for partnerships that drive sustainable agricultural development, especially in underserved regions. The event highlighted the power of collective action in driving change and shaping a resilient future for agrifood systems. The CGIAR Food Systems Accelerator Program is a collaborative effort made possible through the support and partnership of several key organizations. We would like to express our sincere gratitude to the following programs and institutions for their invaluable contributions: CGIAR Initiative on Diversification in East and Southern Africa (Ukama Ustawi). Title: The Soybean Innovation Lab (SIL), in partnership with the International Institute for Tropical Agriculture (IITA), has successfully registered the first publicly bred soybean variety: TGx2014-16FM in The Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) catalog
Description: The Soybean Innovation Lab (SIL), in partnership with the International Institute for Tropical Agriculture (IITA), has successfully registered the first publicly bred soybean variety: TGx2014-16FM. IITA, a CGIAR Research Center based in Ibadan, Nigeria and Lusaka, Zambia, leveraged SIL’s Pan African Trial (PAT) platform to prove the superiority of 16FM across many regions of Sub-Saharan Africa and to provide the scientific data necessary for registration. With its inclusion in the COMESA Variety Catalog, TGx2014-16FM is now available for commercialization across all 21 COMESA member states: Burundi, Comoros, DRC, Djibouti, Egypt, Eritrea, Eswatini, Ethiopia, Kenya, Libya, Madagascar, Malawi, Mauritius, Rwanda, Seychelles, Somalia, Sudan, Tunisia, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. This extensive coverage will facilitate efficient seed distribution and lower costs for farmers throughout the region.

The Soybean Innovation Lab (SIL), in partnership with the International Institute for Tropical Agriculture (IITA), has successfully registered the first publicly bred soybean variety: TGx2014-16FM. COMESA: Transforming the Seed System in Africa The Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) is a regional trade organization that streamlines and accelerates the flow of new seed varieties to farmers. In July 2024, COMESA accepted the registration of 16FM in Malawi and Zambia, as sufficient evidence of the product s value and performance. Once in the catalogue, IITA will directly license 16FM with clients in the other 19 countries of COMESA. This regional registration approach dramatically reduces the cost and time associated with registering a seed product country by country. Farmers also benefit from the regional strategy, with lower seed costs as well as access to a regular and rapid flow of improved varieties with superior yield and disease resistance. This extensive coverage will facilitate efficient seed distribution and lower costs for farmers throughout the region. The PAT platform contains 401 soybean varieties tested by originators and licensees across 30 countries and over 200 locations, with a soybean performance database of over 1.8 million data points. The PAT platform s cooperative network structure lowers the cost and speeds up the time to market for originators and licensees. PATs allow originators like IITA to rapidly evaluate, register, and target their products for licensing into new markets. Licensees, such as seed companies, nucleus farms, and cooperatives, use the PATs to quickly and affordably identify new and improved products to bring to their smallholder farmers. Since 2019, 27 new varieties have been commercialized, with an additional 45 products in the pipeline. Marrying the PATs with the regional catalogue system COMESA (Eastern and South Africa), SADC (Southern Africa), and ECOWAS (West Africa) breaks the log jam of varietal release and brings farmers exciting new products that improve productivity and profitability and spur rural economic development. Title: Ukama Ustawi ShareFair to drive agricultural transformation in Ethiopia
Description: The Ukama Ustawi Share Fair was a two-day event (10-11 December 2024) structured into a series of interactive and participatory sessions aimed at fostering collaboration, sharing lessons and exploring solutions to advance agricultural innovation and food systems transformation in Ethiopia. More importantly, the Share Fair acted as bridge between the current set of CGIAR initiatives and the new portfolio for 2025–2030. The event was led by Ukama Ustawi’s Learning Alliance which connects to the new CGIAR scaling for impact accelerator, highlighting the continuity and strategic alignment of these initiatives.

Foresight Online Economic Modelling Training Course
Overview
The CGIAR Foresight Initiative aims to enhance the modeling capacity of the participants who undertake the courses and the institutions from which they come. From an institutional perspective, it is important to build a solid institutional modeling framework. By training all three types of model users, i.e. senior policy managers, policy analysts, modeling specialists in an institution, you create a solid capacity for understanding model results; analysts that can run and interpret models; and model specialists that can develop and adapt models. A cohesive training program, like the one we have developed, sets a framework for good institutional modeling practices. It leads to consistency in model use across the institution with the hope to sustain the institution's capacity over time.
The Foresight Initiative invested in the development of an Online Economic Modeling Training Course. This led to the design of a modular online training course with seven modules. These seven modules cover introduction to models and economic modeling, and two separate tracks for multi-market modeling with partial equilibrium (PE) models and computable general equilibrium (CGE) models and modeling.
Target audience
The course is designed for ministry workers and policy analysts, networks and research institutes, and university students at the master's and doctorate levels and acknowledges three types of model users: (1) Senior policy managers, (2) Regular policy analysts, and (3) Modeling specialists.

For the course to be efficient and with useful peer exchanges the size of the group of trainees is at minimum 15 and maximum 20 participants.

Foresight Online Economic Modelling Training Course
Overview
The CGIAR Foresight Initiative aims to enhance the modeling capacity of the participants who undertake the courses and the institutions from which they come. From an institutional perspective, it is important to build a solid institutional modeling framework. By training all three types of model users, i.e. senior policy managers, policy analysts, modeling specialists in an institution, you create a solid capacity for understanding model results; analysts that can run and interpret models; and model specialists that can develop and adapt models. A cohesive training program, like the one we have developed, sets a framework for good institutional modeling practices. It leads to consistency in model use across the institution with the hope to sustain the institution's capacity over time.
The Foresight Initiative invested in the development of an Online Economic Modeling Training Course. This led to the design of a modular online training course with seven modules. These seven modules cover introduction to models and economic modeling, and two separate tracks for multi-market modeling with partial equilibrium (PE) models and computable general equilibrium (CGE) models and modeling.
Target audience
The course is designed for ministry workers and policy analysts, networks and research institutes, and university students at the master's and doctorate levels and acknowledges three types of model users: (1) Senior policy managers, (2) Regular policy analysts, and (3) Modeling specialists.

Enhancing collaboration and expertise
The CGIAR Climate Adaptation and Mitigation Impact Area Platform was established in 2023 with a mandate to convene CGIAR’s climate scientists and synthesize climate research to enhance the capacity of CGIAR and its partners. In addition, it will amplify external visibility, engage with prominent climate voices, provide advice on portfolio-level management and strategy, and monitor the climate-related outcomes of various Initiatives.
Central to our mission, we compiled a comprehensive database of almost 600 CGIAR scientists involved in climate-related work across CGIAR’s 14 Centers. On April 12, 2024, the Platform officially launched the CGIAR Climate Community of Practice (CoP). The launch had two sessions ( 9 am and 5 pm GMT) to accommodate the diverse needs of our community across multiple time zones..

Who is in our Community of Practice?
Our CoP has a rich geographic and thematic diversity. Members are located in 24 countries and in the Systems Office. Over a third of our climate scientists are based in India (15.13%), Kenya (10.76%), Colombia (5.71%), and the Philippines (5.38%). Regarding expertise and aspects of climate change, our Community of Practice Climate Scientists work covers a broad array of subjects, from Impacts, Adaptation, Vulnerability, Mitigation, Physical basis of climate change and Climate Finance.
Why It Matters
CGIAR’s collective climate challenge is producing healthy, sustainable, and nutritious food for food and nutrition security and resilience of small-scale food producers while keeping global temperature levels within 1.5°C to 2°C. We are proud to say that the Climate Impact Platform likely hosts the largest community of climate scientists.
The Climate Community of Practice is utilizing collective expertise to develop resilient food systems and sustainable environmental practices. In addition, it connects an international network of experts, promotes collaboration, data sharing, the exchange of best practices and methodologies, and provides an avenue for thematic discussions.

At the launch, CGIAR Executive Managing Director Ismahane Elouafi highlighted agriculture’s often-overlooked role in addressing the climate crisis. “Together this will make consistent and complementary efforts to pull our diverse parts together and have a cohesive narrative on the most important development issues of our day, which is really adaptation to climate change,” she said, noting that this collaborative platform will further unite scientists and drive innovation for improved funding opportunities as part of the new CGIAR 2025-30 portfolio.
Guillaume Grosso, Deputy Executive Managing Director of CGIAR, commented on the impressive scale of the CoP: “Six hundred people identified within CGIAR as working on climate when there was the survey on self- identification, which is amazing; it is one of the largest scientific communities working on climate that I know of,” he said. With Sarah Schmidt, GIZ’s Advisor for International Agricultural Research, outlining the strategic role of the CoP “Germany has supported CGIAR for 50 years, and we see a major role for this community of practice at the science-policy interface, helping to distill and disseminate research findings effectively.”
Building Capacity and Advancing Climate Science
To support ongoing learning and collaboration among CoP members, CGIAR Climate Impact Platform introduced a range of knowledge products designed to build capacity and encourage partnerships within the community. Targeted activities enhanced members' capabilities, enabling CGIAR scientists to contribute to global discussions, scientific assessments, and climate negotiations. This year, the Platform launched a webinar series to showcase CGIAR research, build member capacity, and promote collaboration with external climate scientists. We covered four critical climate topics this year on areas CGIAR has not done extensive work on- Loss and Damage, Carbon Credits, Carbon Dioxide Removals and Global Goals Adaptation.

The inaugural webinar on 25 March asked the question: How can attribution science inform loss and damage? From at the Grantham Institute for Climate Change and the Environment, Dr. Friederike Otto discussed legal and policy implications of attribution science as a useful tool for loss and damage attribution. Dr Joyce Kimutai, from the Grantham Institute for Climate Change and the Environment and the Kenya Meteorological Department, noted the need for different ways of determining loss and damage in contexts where data may be lacking.
Each webinar has been tailored to further participants’ understanding of important new developments in climate policy and science, with implications for their work. In the second webinar: Loss and Damage: understanding its past, present and future, Dr. Animesh Kumar, Head of the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR), and Ms. Teresa Anderson, Global Lead on Climate Justice at ActionAid International, explored historical consequences of climate change and implications of climate justice.
In webinar three, “CGIAR Climate Impact Area Webinar Series - Webinar 3: Carbon Credits: Can they be fixed?” Yale Environmental Economist Professor Rohini Pande and Dr Danny Cullenward explored the topic of carbon offset surging a shift in “business as usual” thinking, towards global climate targets. Dr Danny Cullenward, from the Institute of Carbon Removal Law and Policy, American University, Washington, DC, and the Kleinman Center for Energy Policy at the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, weighed in on how and why carbon offsets are currently incompatible with the Paris Agreements.
Webinar four focused on “Adaptation and carbon dioxide removal in a warming world,” with Dr Tabea Lissner, Research Director, Global Solutions Initiative and a Lead Author of the 6th IPCC Assessment, exploring what will happen if we surpass the 1.5°C temperature threshold enshrined in the Paris Agreement, especially implications for the world’s most vulnerable communities. Dr. Annette Cowie, Principal Research Scientist at NSW Department of Primary Industries, a lead author of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Special Report on Climate Change and Land, and another lead author of the 6th IPCC Assessment, demystified carbon dioxide removal.
Webinar five focused on “Measuring the effectiveness of adaptation insights from the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) and the Global Environment Facility (GEF) projects,” explored tools and methods used to measure adaptation effectiveness and resilience. Dr. Jyotsna Puri, Associate Vice-President of the Strategy and Knowledge Department at IFAD, discussed resilience credits; while Professor Ed Carr, Centre Director and Senior Scientist at SEI US, shared discussed indicators used in global adaptation goals and why measuring adaptation progress is crucial for effective adaptation strategies.
Finally, webinar six: “Tracking global adaptation: Indicators and LDC priorities at COP29,” brought together three experts to reflect on the shift from defining an overarching goal for climate adaptation to identifying indicators that can be implemented globally. Dr Timo Leiter, from the Grantham Research Institute at the London School of Economics (LSE), spoke about UNFCCC process; Dr Luckson Zvobgo, postdoctoral research fellow, at the Africa Climate and Development Initiative, University of Cape Town, emphasized that adaptation indicators need to realistic, actionable, and reflective of context; and Dr Cristina Rumbaitis del Rio, Senior Advisor for Adaptation and Resilience at the United Nations Foundation, explained how to elevate adaptation ambition at COP-29 and beyond.
Enhancing Knowledge and Engagement Among the CoP
The Platform has implemented a variety of activities to deepen engagement within the Climate Community of Practice (CoP) and address knowledge gaps. Smaller thematic working groups were introduced to focus on specific climate issues, while quarterly meetings provided opportunities for discussions on topics like how to engage in IPCC processes, emerging trends in climate science, and updates on CGIAR’s global priorities.
In 2024, the Platform launched Climate Insights, a fortnightly roundup of cutting-edge publications on climate change impacts, adaptation, mitigation measures, and physical science. By the end of December, 23 editions were published, featuring over 550 papers covering diverse topics such as food security and building climate-resilient systems. 73% of respondents to our end of year survey reported that they use Climate Insights to support their work Very Often (2%), Often (24%), and Sometimes (47%). Additionally, the bi-monthly newsletters offered updates on Platform activities, emerging climate trends and research, success stories from CGIAR Centers and Initiatives, and profiles of CoP members.

To keep CoP members informed about global climate policies and negotiations, the Platform published 11 daily briefs during the Bonn Climate Conference and 13 during COP29. These provided timely updates and expert analysis of negotiation processes and outcomes. 47% of respondents to our end of year survey reported that the knowledge products shared during COP29 were Extremely Useful or Somewhat Useful for their work.
The development of a centralized SharePoint site created a one-stop hub for CGIAR climate scientists to access resources, share knowledge products, and engage in communication. The CGIAR Climate Community of Practice officially kicked into gear in April 2024, marking a significant step towards CGIAR Climate Impact Platform's progress in delivering on its mandate to convene CGIAR climate scientists and synthesize climate research to enhance the capacity of CGIAR and its partners. Taking efforts to facilitate collaboration between the CGIAR climate community one step further, the Climate Impact Platform launched the CGIAR Climate Community Dgroups platform.
The CGIAR Climate Community Dgroups was created with the goal of facilitating regular, open, productive dialogues for the CGIAR scientists and partners that make up the Climate Community of Practice. Serving as an open forum for discussions and ideas - we are using the platform to connect our 500+ CGIAR scientists working in the climate space, share knowledge products and information around climate-related events and updates, and convene thematic discussions on climate issues relevant to the work being done at CGIAR.
Convening the Climate Community in Thematic Discussions & Subgroups
Thematic Discussions
One of the primary functions of the Climate Community Dgroups is to share and discuss ideas on relevant, emerging research topics and issues. Since the launch of the platform, we have facilitated three thematic discussions on the following topics:
1) Role of carbon credits in achieving climate goals
As rising temperatures and rapidly escalating weather emergencies convince the global community that urgent steps must be taken to reduce emissions, private actors have responded with a voluntary system for companies and project developers to buy and sell carbon credits. This commentary urges that the fact that a market collapsed in 2023 should not put us off. A close look at how it was designed shows that it was destined to fail—and a close look at alternative markets shows that it could work.
This first discussion presented the questions posted by Professor Rohini Pande, in her latest commentary for Science: Are voluntary carbon markets inevitably a hoax allowing companies to continue emitting high levels of CO2 and other greenhouse gases that may be included in these markets, while using ineffective, low-cost offsets to maintain the pretense that they’re meeting their own climate targets, thus undermining efforts to prevent climate breakdown? Or are they an effective way to channel funds to projects that can reduce global emissions quickly and cheaply?
2) Reducing emissions in agriculture through breakthrough technologies
The 2024 Breakthrough Agenda Report - Agriculture, the first in the series to focus exclusively on the agricultural sector, taps into CGIAR’s expertise, alongside that of global stakeholders, to assess the current state of international collaboration on sustainable agricultural practices. It also offers actionable recommendations for governments and non-state actors to drive meaningful change in the sector.
The report zeroes in on the two biggest sources of emissions in agrifood systems—fertilizers and livestock—and presents four concrete technologies for reducing emissions: methane inhibitors, low-methane forages, green ammonia, and site-specific nutrient management (SSNM). Responses in this discussion touched on how the adoption of these four technologies can help achieve global climate goals, the barriers to scaling these solutions,

and how CGIAR's research can support the deployment of these technologies to transform agriculture into a climate-resilient, low-emissions system.
3) Contributing to the Future of Climate Action: CGIAR’s Participation at COP29
At the Food & Agriculture Pavilion at COP29, CGIAR and FAO created a platform for collaborative dialogue, knowledge sharing, and decision-making on the unique role of agriculture and food systems in the fight against climate change. From hosting 44+ events at the Food and Agriculture Pavilion to leading 8 official UN Climate Change sessions, including a key session on Food and Agriculture Day, we championed the integration of science and innovation into climate solutions. Our team also launched 9 Issue Briefs, produced 11 Daily Briefs, and shared critical reflections, ensuring that the intersections of food systems, finance, and equity were well-represented in global discussions.
As the curtains closed on COP29 in Baku, this discussion reflected on two weeks of intense negotiations, side events, and critical discussions.
Thematic Subgroups
Beyond participating in thematic discussions, the Climate Platform further facilitated the creation of two thematic subgroups that members can join on the following two topics: Climate change impacts and adaptation and Climate change mitigation. The topics of these subgroups were based on the suggestions provided directly by the Community of Practice through a survey that was distributed in 2024.
1. Climate change impacts and adaptation subgroup
Climate change is affecting nature, people’s lives and infrastructure everywhere. It's dangerous and pervasive impacts are increasingly evident in every region of our world, and are hindering efforts to meet basic human needs. To deal with climate hazards and reduce risks for people and ecosystems that come from climate change, we have to adapt – but progress is uneven and large gaps exist between adaptation action taken and what is needed in many regions.
2. Climate change mitigation subgroup
Avoiding and reducing emissions of heat-trapping greenhouse gases into the atmosphere is critical to prevent the planet from warming to even more extreme temperatures. Effective mitigation strategies require an understanding of mechanisms that underpin release of emissions, and the technical, policy and societal options for influencing these.
Engaging Systematic Review Methods Training Alumni
In 2024, the Climate Impact Platform hosted eight Systematic Review Methods Trainings to strengthen the capacity of CGIAR scientists, National Agricultural Research and Extension Systems (NARES), and African Group on Negotiators Experts Support (AGNES) partners. These workshops introduced systematic reviewing and systematic mapping as methods for evidence synthesis, providing participants with the opportunity to gain an in-depth understanding of the necessary activities to maximize comprehensiveness, transparency, objectivity, and reliability throughout the review process.
To continue engaging the 200+ participants after their successful completion of the training, the Climate Platform launched the Systematic Review Methods Training Alumni subgroup on Dgroups.
The alumni group will continue to serve as an open forum to connect participants from all training cohorts and provide a platform for discussing current systematic review projects, posing questions and challenges, and exploring opportunities for collaboration.

Impact Story 4
The CGIAR Climate Community of Practice officially kicked into gear in April 2024, marking a significant step towards CGIAR Climate Impact Platform's progress in delivering on its mandate to convene CGIAR climate scientists and synthesize climate research to enhance the capacity of CGIAR and its partners. Taking efforts to facilitate collaboration between the CGIAR climate community one step further, the Climate Impact Platform launched the CGIAR Climate Community Dgroups platform.
The CGIAR Climate Community Dgroups was created with the goal of facilitating regular, open, productive dialogues for the CGIAR scientists and partners that make up the Climate Community of Practice. Serving as an open forum for discussions and ideas - we are using the platform to connect our 500+ CGIAR scientists working in the climate space, share knowledge products and information around climate-related events and updates, and convene thematic discussions on climate issues relevant to the work being done at CGIAR.
Convening the Climate Community in Thematic Discussions & Subgroups
Thematic Discussions
One of the primary functions of the Climate Community Dgroups is to share and discuss ideas on relevant, emerging research topics and issues. Since the launch of the platform, we have facilitated three thematic discussions on the following topics:
1) Role of carbon credits in achieving climate goals
As rising temperatures and rapidly escalating weather emergencies convince the global community that urgent steps must be taken to reduce emissions, private actors have responded with a voluntary system for companies and project developers to buy and sell carbon credits. This commentary urges that the fact that a market collapsed in 2023 should not put us off. A close look at how it was designed shows that it was destined to fail—and a close look at alternative markets shows that it could work.
This first discussion presented the questions posted by Professor Rohini Pande, in her latest commentary for Science: Are voluntary carbon markets inevitably a hoax allowing companies to continue emitting high levels of CO2 and other greenhouse gases that may be included in these markets, while using ineffective, low-cost offsets to maintain the pretense that they’re meeting their own climate targets, thus undermining efforts to prevent climate breakdown? Or are they an effective way to channel funds to projects that can reduce global emissions quickly and cheaply?
2) Reducing emissions in agriculture through breakthrough technologies
The 2024 Breakthrough Agenda Report - Agriculture, the first in the series to focus exclusively on the agricultural sector, taps into CGIAR’s expertise, alongside that of global stakeholders, to assess the current state of international collaboration on sustainable agricultural practices. It also offers actionable recommendations for governments and non-state actors to drive meaningful change in the sector.
The report zeroes in on the two biggest sources of emissions in agrifood systems—fertilizers and livestock—and presents four concrete technologies for reducing emissions: methane inhibitors, low-methane forages, green ammonia, and site-specific nutrient management (SSNM). Responses in this discussion touched on how the adoption of these four technologies can help achieve global climate goals, the barriers to scaling these solutions,

and how CGIAR's research can support the deployment of these technologies to transform agriculture into a climate-resilient, low-emissions system.
3) Contributing to the Future of Climate Action: CGIAR’s Participation at COP29
At the Food & Agriculture Pavilion at COP29, CGIAR and FAO created a platform for collaborative dialogue, knowledge sharing, and decision-making on the unique role of agriculture and food systems in the fight against climate change. From hosting 44+ events at the Food and Agriculture Pavilion to leading 8 official UN Climate Change sessions, including a key session on Food and Agriculture Day, we championed the integration of science and innovation into climate solutions. Our team also launched 9 Issue Briefs, produced 11 Daily Briefs, and shared critical reflections, ensuring that the intersections of food systems, finance, and equity were well-represented in global discussions.
As the curtains closed on COP29 in Baku, this discussion reflected on two weeks of intense negotiations, side events, and critical discussions.
Thematic Subgroups
Beyond participating in thematic discussions, the Climate Platform further facilitated the creation of two thematic subgroups that members can join on the following two topics: Climate change impacts and adaptation and Climate change mitigation. The topics of these subgroups were based on the suggestions provided directly by the Community of Practice through a survey that was distributed in 2024.
1. Climate change impacts and adaptation subgroup
Climate change is affecting nature, people’s lives and infrastructure everywhere. It's dangerous and pervasive impacts are increasingly evident in every region of our world, and are hindering efforts to meet basic human needs. To deal with climate hazards and reduce risks for people and ecosystems that come from climate change, we have to adapt – but progress is uneven and large gaps exist between adaptation action taken and what is needed in many regions.
2. Climate change mitigation subgroup
Avoiding and reducing emissions of heat-trapping greenhouse gases into the atmosphere is critical to prevent the planet from warming to even more extreme temperatures. Effective mitigation strategies require an understanding of mechanisms that underpin release of emissions, and the technical, policy and societal options for influencing these.
Engaging Systematic Review Methods Training Alumni
In 2024, the Climate Impact Platform hosted eight Systematic Review Methods Trainings to strengthen the capacity of CGIAR scientists, National Agricultural Research and Extension Systems (NARES), and African Group on Negotiators Experts Support (AGNES) partners. These workshops introduced systematic reviewing and systematic mapping as methods for evidence synthesis, providing participants with the opportunity to gain an in-depth understanding of the necessary activities to maximize comprehensiveness, transparency, objectivity, and reliability throughout the review process.
To continue engaging the 200+ participants after their successful completion of the training, the Climate Platform launched the Systematic Review Methods Training Alumni subgroup on Dgroups.
The alumni group will continue to serve as an open forum to connect participants from all training cohorts and provide a platform for discussing current systematic review projects, posing questions and challenges, and exploring opportunities for collaboration.

CGIAR Climate Impact Platform
Impact Report 2
In 2024, the CGIAR Climate Impact Platform launched its collaboration with the Juno Evidence Alliance to support our ongoing efforts to conduct high quality, rigorous systematic review of climate change related work across agrifood systems in Africa and Asia. Synthesizing published literature in the climate change and agri-food systems space and to use that synthesis to influence science agenda is one of the central functions of the CGIAR’s Climate Impact Platform. The collaboration stemmed from the recognition of the need for mentorship and guidance in developing outputs that address critical knowledge gaps identified from previous assessments of CGIAR climate- related research. By providing mentorship and guidance on the development of four systematic review protocols that the CGIAR’s Climate Impact Platform commissioned in 2024, Juno Evidence Alliance is working with the Platform to help implement high quality research, address critical knowledge gaps, and improve the CGIAR's capacity to do rigorous evidence synthesis.

The following four reviews have been commissioned by the CGIAR Climate Impact Platform:
o Review 1: The impact of agricultural information services on farm household outcomes in Sub-Saharan Africa (Lead: Dr. Solomon Zena Walelign, University of Gondar, Ethiopia)
o Review 2: What evidence exists on the pathways linking climate change to livestock production and consumption in Sub-Saharan Africa? (Lead: Dr. Amare Abera Tareke, Wollo University, Ethiopia)
o Review 3: How effective are adaptation practices on offsetting sorghum and millet yield reductions under climate change (Lead: Prof. Irenikatche Akponikpe, Insititute for Science and Technology Innovation in Africa, Benin)
o Review 4: The role of digital and climate-smart agriculture in climate change mitigation: a systematic mapping protocol for South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa (Lead: Dr. Maaz Gardezi, Virginia Tech University)

2
The overall purpose of the collaboration is to strengthen the research rigor for systematic reviews in the environmental field. The use of systematic reviews to represent information is more advanced in the field of health research and there is a growing need for these skills and capacities in the field of environmental research. The Climate Platform built on the collaboration with the Collaboration for Environmental Evidence (CEE) who partnered to nurturing a cohort of environmental evidence assessors though Systematic Review Methods trainings. Building on the feedback from the training sessions, the Platform then engaged with the Juno Evidence Alliance in more advance skills mentorship for the systematic review outputs with four grantees.
Key outcomes of the engagement with the Juno Evidence Alliance
The partnership with Juno Evidence Alliance has led to significant milestones:
1. Development and systematic review protocols
Rigorous methodologies were followed in the creation of four high-quality systematic map and review protocols. Key activities included:
o Stakeholder engagement to validating methods and assessing the relevance of proposed solutions and recommendations.
o Productive iterations through continuous collaboration between the four review teams and the Juno Evidence Alliance Team. Learn more about Juno’s work here.
o Finalization and publication of protocols ensuring the protocols meet the systematic review standards before publishing it on CGIAR's online repository, CGSpace.
o Future engagement with the team will include mentorship to the review teams on developing systematic map either as reports or publishable manuscripts. The reports will provide a comprehensive outline of overarching results from the systematic mapping of literature in the topical areas of the four reviews.
2. Strengthening CGIAR Climate Platform's evidence synthesis expertise and activities
The collaboration has strengthened the technical capacity of team members, enabling them to produce tools and outputs that meet rigorous academic and scientific standards. These products can then be adapted into accessible formats such as blog posts, policy briefs, maps, illustrations, and presentations tailored to diverse audiences.
3. Building capacity of the CGIAR Climate Community of Practice and expanding Research Networks
This collaboration with Juno Evidence Alliance follows the successful delivery of eight Systematic Review Methods Training to 221 selected CGIAR scientists, NARES, and AGNES partners. The trainings were designed to strengthen the capacity of the CGIAR Climate Community of Practice and partners by equipping participants with a thorough understanding of systematic review and systematic map methods. Thanks to the engagement with CEE, the 200+ participants that completed the Systematic Review Methods Training now have the skills necessary to plan and execute a review project effectively. The engagement further broadened the CGIAR Climate Community of Practice's network of agricultural and environmental research partners to include organizations such as CABI and the Collaboration for Environmental Evidence (CEE). Explore more about CEE here.
This collaboration with Juno Evidence Alliance envisions further training in 2025, to include both basic training and advanced training for a new cohort of trainings and the alumni of the first round of trainings, respectively. Additionally, the success of the current collaboration encourages further and broader expansion of the current activities to include the commissioning of a new round of grants for systematic reviews based on lessons learnt from the four studies already underway.
Overall, this collaboration aims to support the objectives of minimizing the duplication of efforts across CGIAR centres and enhancing the understanding of how climate research aligns with both organizational and global climate change goals. By leaning into the opportunity for guided interaction with evidence synthesis tools, the Platform has worked with Juno Evidence Alliance to not only created a robust evidence base of current research but also identified future research agendas for CGIAR institutions, government partners, and donors. This effort is pivotal in ensuring that research contributes effectively to climate adaptation and mitigation strategies in the agri- food sector.

In 2024, the CGIAR Climate Impact Platform launched its collaboration with the Juno Evidence Alliance to support our ongoing efforts to conduct high quality, rigorous systematic review of climate change related work across agrifood systems in Africa and Asia. Synthesizing published literature in the climate change and agri-food systems space and to use that synthesis to influence science agenda is one of the central functions of the CGIAR’s Climate Impact Platform. The collaboration stemmed from the recognition of the need for mentorship and guidance in developing outputs that address critical knowledge gaps identified from previous assessments of CGIAR climate- related research. By providing mentorship and guidance on the development of four systematic review protocols that the CGIAR’s Climate Impact Platform commissioned in 2024, Juno Evidence Alliance is working with the Platform to help implement high quality research, address critical knowledge gaps, and improve the CGIAR's capacity to do rigorous evidence synthesis.

The following four reviews have been commissioned by the CGIAR Climate Impact Platform:
o Review 1: The impact of agricultural information services on farm household outcomes in Sub-Saharan Africa (Lead: Dr. Solomon Zena Walelign, University of Gondar, Ethiopia)
o Review 2: What evidence exists on the pathways linking climate change to livestock production and consumption in Sub-Saharan Africa? (Lead: Dr. Amare Abera Tareke, Wollo University, Ethiopia)
o Review 3: How effective are adaptation practices on offsetting sorghum and millet yield reductions under climate change (Lead: Prof. Irenikatche Akponikpe, Insititute for Science and Technology Innovation in Africa, Benin)
o Review 4: The role of digital and climate-smart agriculture in climate change mitigation: a systematic mapping protocol for South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa (Lead: Dr. Maaz Gardezi, Virginia Tech University)
